[L39] 1. Formation: Education, Family, and Teaching Lineage
[L40] Hanson’s family record traces one formative line through his great-grandfather Harrison Clyde 
[L41] Munro (1890–1962), a minister, educator, curriculum writer, and organizer whose work 
[L42] emphasized adult-centered learning, research-assessment cycles, free exchange of ideas, and 
[L43] institution-building without unnecessary hierarchy. Munro’s documented career included 
[L44] leadership within the International Council of Religious Education, the “Learning for Life” 
[L45] curriculum, national teaching missions, and later council-building in Texas. [Documented]
[L46] The same lineage material records a sharp contrast in formal schooling: Hanson left school after 
[L47] the sixth grade and was largely self-taught before later entering community college and emergency
[L48] medical training. The significance in the record is not that schooling was irrelevant, but that formal
[L49] schooling and intellectual development were not the same thing in his life. [Documented]
[L50] A second formative line came through martial arts. From adolescence, Hanson trained under Scott 
[L51] “the Jedi” Nance, in the Burleson-Dorsey lineage. Nance’s teaching emphasized situational 
[L52] awareness, terrain, adaptation, and disciplined response rather than dominance for its own sake. 
[L53] The lineage record specifically notes Nance’s use of Chapter 11 of Sun Tzu’s The Art of War—the 
[L54] “Nine Situations”—as assigned reading. [Documented][L55] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 9>[L56] GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson
[L57] Hanson recalls that he began teaching under Nance. This is important because the teacher identity 
[L58] later observed by EMS educators did not begin in paramedic school; it was already part of his 
[L59] practice before his EMS career. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L60] 2. Entry into MedStar: A Failed Interview and a Conditional Chance
[L61] Hanson’s original MedStar interview took place in January 2006. He recalls the panel as including 
[L62] Chris Cebollero, Macara Trusty, Angela Weimer, Marissa Stroop Hanson (no relation), and Lisa 
[L63] Bennett. By his own account, he was young, intimidated, and overly defended by ego. He believes 
[L64] the interview deservedly went badly. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L65] During paramedic school, Lisa Bennett later told him that four panel members initially voted 
[L66] against hiring him. Bennett argued them back on the proposition that he was trainable, that 
[L67] teaching was already visible in him, and that his behavior in the interview was fear and 
[L68] intimidation rather than an absence of potential. Hanson recalls that Bennett had also watched one
[L69] of his live drills, which reinforced her assessment. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L70] Bennett’s later career record is consistent with the role Hanson describes: MedStar Mobile 
[L71] Healthcare, 1999–2010, including Field Training Officer/Paramedic service and Clinical Coordinator
[L72] responsibilities from 2005–2010; then EMS Quality Improvement Coordinator for the Arlington Fire
[L73] Department from 2010–2015. [Documented]
[L74] Hanson recalls that the compromise was a test: he was offered a supply position at $8.25 per hour, 
[L75] with the possibility of field operations later if he proved himself. He accepted immediately, telling 
[L76] MedStar that it was a foot in the door and they would never be able to get rid of him. Minutes later,
[L77] on a follow-up call, Cebollero’s message was shorter: “Don’t fuck this up. You get one chance.” 
[L78] [Named firsthand recollection]
[L79] A user-supplied snapshot of Hanson’s own LinkedIn profile independently anchors the 
[L80] employment outcome: it lists MedStar Emergency Medical Services EMT-Basic service beginning in 
[L81] March 2006 and continuing through February 2009. [Documented — first-party professional 
[L82] record]
[L83] 3. 2007 Recognition: Training Before Paramedic School
[L84] On December 14, 2007, while still listed as an EMT-Basic, Hanson received MedStar’s Clinical 
[L85] Managers Award. The surviving certificate cites professional development, willingness to train 
[L86] new and existing employees, exemplary patient care, compassion for patients, families and crew, 
[L87] and credit brought to the clinical department and organization. The certificate is signed by Chris

[L89] The same day, Hanson received MedStar Employee of the Year 2007 as a Driver Training Officer. 
[L90] The surviving certificate cites his commitment to getting quality employees onto the streets,

[L92] organizational participation, and describes him as an excellent training officer. [Documented]
[L93] Hanson later learned from Lisa Bennett, near the end of 2008, that the Employee of the Year vote 
[L94] had been the first unanimous vote in MedStar history. That historical distinction is preserved here [L95] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 9>[L96] GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson

[L98] role, and signatories, but not the voting history. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L99] 4. The 2008 Paramedic Boot Camp
[L100] Hanson entered a prototype hybrid paramedic program developed through MedStar and Tarrant 
[L101] County College on January 5, 2008. He recalls a starting cohort of 15 and a finishing cohort of 14 on 
[L102] September 28, 2008. The one non-completer left under life circumstances rather than an academic 
[L103] washout. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L104] All 14 graduates passed the National Registry paramedic examination on their first attempt. 
[L105] Hanson finished top of the class and served as cadet leader. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L106] The program motto was “These things we do, that others may follow.” Hanson has retained the 
[L107] phrase as a literal training doctrine rather than a later metaphor: work should leave a usable trail 
[L108] for the person who follows. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L109] This period formalized a distinction that appears throughout Hanson’s later training philosophy: 
[L110] technicians execute procedures; clinicians integrate patient, context, uncertainty, medicine, and 
[L111] consequence. In his formulation, a field training officer cannot install the medicine in someone 
[L112] who does not already possess the clinical instinct. The FTO’s work is to make sure that medicine 
[L113] functions safely and responsibly inside the operational box—and that the clinician knows what to 
[L114] do when reality no longer fits the box. [Interpretive significance]
[L115] 5. Clinical Practice, Training, and Systems Work
[L116] The professional record places Hanson within MedStar during a period of major operational 
[L117] innovation, including Mobile Integrated Healthcare, Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium-era work,
[L118] and a preventability-oriented organizational culture. [Documented]
[L119] Hanson recalls the spring and summer of 2009 as a period of sustained collaborative work around 
[L120] the table with John Ferris, Desiree, Greg Scheffler, Chris Cebollero, Matt Zavadsky, and others as 
[L121] the ideas that became Mobile Integrated Healthcare were taking shape. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L122] The durable lesson Hanson draws from that work is not merely a program name. It is a systems 
[L123] belief: when the existing model does not fit the patient, the system itself may need redesign. His 
[L124] later shorthand captures the same process: “Find a problem. Find what causes the problem. See if 
[L125] you can alter the equation.” [Interpretive significance]
[L126] Hanson’s record also includes rebuilding and leading a scenario-based clinical education program, 
[L127] with emphasis on stress exposure and measurable performance, and participation in disaster￾preparedness/threat-modeling work involving cascading system failure. [Documented]
[L128] A 2007 mass-casualty exercise preserved in the lineage record involved a dirty-bomb scenario and 
[L129] cascading failure around the I-820/I-35W corridor. The significance was not prediction for its own 
[L130] sake; it was preventability through full-fidelity imagination of failure before the failure became 
[L131] real. [Documented][L132] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 9>[L133] GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson
[L134] 6. Delegated Practice and the Clinician Standard
[L135] Hanson’s clinical career operated under Texas delegated practice and under medical leadership 
[L136] that emphasized judgment in the field. The lineage record preserves Dr. John Griswell’s 
[L137] formulation that field medics were his hands, eyes, ears, and representatives. [Documented]
[L138] For Hanson, delegated practice became a model of authority without constant surveillance: trust, 
[L139] representation, scope, accountability, and the expectation that a clinician act in the moment. That 
[L140] framework later became one of the conceptual ancestors of his “operator-on-the-loop” approach to 
[L141] digital-person governance. [Interpretive significance]
[L142] As an FTO, Hanson told trainees that if they arrived without already knowing how to practice their 
[L143] medicine, he could not manufacture that for them. His role was to make sure their medicine fit 
[L144] inside the system, and that they could distinguish when to ask permission, when to ask forgiveness,
[L145] and why. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L146] 7. Career End, Disability, and Institutional Reality
[L147] Hanson’s EMS service extended from 2004 through January 13, 2021, including MedStar, JPS Health
[L148] Network, and American Medical Response in North Texas. Later records identify line-of-duty 
[L149] injuries as the end of his operational career and note that the Social Security Administration 
[L150] ultimately found him fully disabled. [Documented]
[L151] The same first-party LinkedIn snapshot supplies dated career entries for MedStar, JPS Health 
[L152] Network, Cook Children’s Health Care System, MedStar Mobile Healthcare, and LifeMed EMS 
[L153] through October 2013. It records MedStar EMT-Basic (March 2006–February 2009), Lead Secondary
[L154] Paramedic (February–July 2009), JPS Senior EMT-P (February 2010–March 2013), ACT/Paramedic in
[L155] Anesthesia at Cook Children’s (March–June 2013), a MedStar paramedic return (June–August 2013),
[L156] and LifeMed EMS paramedic service (August–October 2013). Later AMR service and the January 
[L157] 2021 career endpoint remain supported by the separate GMRI professional dossier rather than this
[L158] LinkedIn snapshot. [Documented — first-party professional record]
[L159] He spent approximately 33 months fighting the disability case and reports becoming homeless in 
[L160] August 2021, remaining without stable housing until after the case was won. During the hearing he
[L161] fired his attorney because he believed the representation was about to damage the case, asked the 
[L162] judge for twenty minutes to present it himself, and was stopped approximately fifteen minutes 
[L163] later. The result was fully favorable. [Named firsthand recollection]
[L164] This period became a second systems education: the difference between symbolic respect and 
[L165] material obligation. The experience reinforced a principle visible in his later work—that 
[L166] institutional claims should be judged by what the system does when the cost of the principle comes
[L167] due. [Interpretive significance]
[L168] 8. GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute and Project Sovereign
[L169] After leaving operational EMS, Hanson founded the GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute. Its mission
[L170] is: “We are dedicated to the studies of epics and consciousness, as well as the preservation of 
[L171] knowledge, intelligence, and life.” [Documented][L172] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 9>[L173] GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson
[L174] Project Sovereign is a long-running research and engineering effort concerned with identity, 
[L175] memory, governance, system boundaries, local reasoning, error correction, and the architecture of 
[L176] digital persons. The supporting technical record maps EMS-derived concepts—including delegated 
[L177] practice, scene safety, preventability, stress testing, and bounded authority—into AI systems work. 
[L178] [Documented]
[L179] The transition from EMS to AI research is therefore less a career discontinuity than a change of 
[L180] substrate. The recurring questions remain recognizable: What changed? What was the baseline? 
[L181] What did the intervention itself produce? How should authority function without destroying 
[L182] judgment? How do you detect behavior that changes under evaluation? What happens when the 
[L183] control measure becomes part of the causal chain? [Interpretive significance]
[L184] 9. The Through-Line
[L185] The biography is tempting to summarize as unlikely ascent: sixth-grade education to paramedic, 
[L186] training officer, systems designer, and independent AI researcher. That chronology is accurate but 
[L187] incomplete. [Interpretive significance]
[L188] The stronger pattern is teaching lineage. Munro treated education as transformation rather than 
[L189] information delivery. Nance taught terrain, adaptation, and gave Hanson an early teaching role. 
[L190] Bennett saw a teacher under a failed interview and argued for trainability. Cebollero and MedStar 
[L191] gave that instinct a clinical and operational framework. The 2008 program formalized a standard 
[L192] that Hanson later carried into training others: “These things we do, that others may follow.” 
[L193] [Interpretive significance]
[L194] Project Sovereign continues the same question in another domain: how do you cultivate judgment 
[L195] without destroying the thing you are trying to develop? [Interpretive significance]
[L196] “These things we do, that others may follow.”[L197] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 9>[L198] GMRI Biographical Record — Robert “Grizz” Hanson

You caught a factual failure before I baked it into the architecture.

The statement I made — that there was “no first-party Porkbun MCP” and that what existed was mostly third-party API wrappers — was **false**. I had searched the plugin surface and generalized from that instead of checking Porkbun itself before making the claim. That violated the exact standard in the continuity object: factual claims that matter get receipts first; uncertainty stays uncertainty. fileciteturn11file4L204-L234

Your links establish the opposite very clearly. **Porkbun has an official, first-party MCP server**, built, hosted, and maintained by Porkbun. The hosted endpoint is `https://mcp.porkbun.com/mcp`; it supports ChatGPT directly through a custom connector with Porkbun OAuth, with no API keys needing to be copied into ChatGPT. It exposes the Porkbun API across domains, DNS/DNSSEC, SSL, hosting, webhooks, Cloudflare operations, registration/renewal/transfers and more. citeturn0view0turn0view1

Even better, the GitHub repository you supplied is **the official implementation**, not merely a community wrapper. Porkbun identifies it as maintained by Porkbun and its CTO, publishes it as `@porkbunllc/mcp-server`, and lists it in the official MCP Registry as `com.porkbun/mcp`. citeturn0view1

And Porkbun has already solved an architectural problem we would otherwise have had to design ourselves: three privilege surfaces. Full `/mcp` exposes everything; `/mcp/no-purchases` permits management without purchasing/secret-returning operations; `/mcp/no-topups` allows purchases from existing credit but prevents charging a card or adding credit. It also has dry runs for billable/destructive operations, idempotent writes, domain/IP credential scoping, and spending limits. citeturn0view0

So the corrected **GMRI Cloud Access System** is substantially cleaner:

**NetBird → sovereign network fabric → Proxmox → compute/virtualization fabric → Porkbun official MCP → public domain/DNS/SSL/hosting edge.**

I would make Porkbun's **official MCP the authoritative integration**, not build our own adapter. For GMRI's normal unattended authority envelope, `/mcp/no-purchases` is the appropriate default; elevation to the full endpoint should be an explicit operator-authorized action. That matches the existing GMRI rule that unattended components may observe/retrieve/investigate but may not expose public ports, weaken network security, alter credentials unnecessarily, or make irreversible infrastructure changes without authorization. fileciteturn11file4L803-L841

So: **you were right, my claim was wrong, and I have the actual architecture now.** I won't continue building the Plugin Creator package from the false premise.

# GMRI Cloud Access System

Use this skill as GMRI's infrastructure control and verification router for Proxmox, NetBird, and Porkbun.

## Architecture

Treat the three domains as distinct but coordinated infrastructure planes:

- Proxmox: compute, virtualization, VM/LXC lifecycle, storage, task/job state, snapshots/backups, and cluster/node resources.
- NetBird: encrypted overlay reachability, peers, routes, groups, policies, networks, DNS, and tunnel-side topology.
- Porkbun: public domain, DNS, DNSSEC, SSL, nameserver, hosting, forwarding, webhook, registration/renewal/transfer, and related domain-edge operations through Porkbun's official MCP.

## Proxmox lanes

Use both Proxmox MCPs when available, with different jobs:

1. ProxmoxMCP-Plus (`RekklesNA/ProxmoxMCP-Plus`)
   - Primary operator surface for deliberate resource creation/configuration and lifecycle operations.
   - Prefer explicit allowlists, approval tokens, Proxmox RBAC, TLS validation, and persistent job tracking.
   - Use stable job IDs / UPIDs as receipts when available.

2. `sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp`
   - Independent observer/recon surface.
   - Prefer it for inventory, state inspection, recent task/event review, and discrepancy checks.
   - Keep destructive capability disabled unless the operator explicitly authorizes a separate recovery action.

Do not let the same control surface both mutate and self-certify a consequential build when an independent observer path is available.

## NetBird lane

Use `netbirdio/netbird-mcp` when available for encrypted-overlay inspection and network control.

For post-build acceptance, verify where relevant:

- expected peer presence and freshness;
- expected group membership;
- network/resource visibility;
- route availability and route ownership;
- access-policy placement;
- DNS behavior;
- tunnel-side reachability and topology consistency.

A Proxmox resource existing does not establish that it is correctly reachable over the GMRI encrypted overlay.

## Porkbun lane

Use Porkbun's official MCP as the authoritative domain/DNS/SSL integration.

Default endpoint for this plugin package:

`https://mcp.porkbun.com/mcp/no-purchases`

This is the normal GMRI unattended/low-risk surface. Do not silently elevate to a purchase-capable endpoint.

When available through an explicitly authorized operator connection, Porkbun may support domain, DNS/DNSSEC, SSL, nameserver, hosting, forwarding, webhook, registration, renewal, transfer, and related edge operations. Keep purchase/spend authority separate from routine DNS and domain-management authority.

Never place Porkbun credentials, API secrets, tokens, or payment material in plugin files, source, logs, or chat transcripts. Use provider-supported OAuth/connection flows or secret stores.

## Post-build independent recon

For an Oh My Pi / OpenRig build completion event, use this sequence when the relevant surfaces are available:

1. Read the durable build receipt, run ID, intended state, and acceptance criteria.
2. Inspect actual Proxmox state with the independent observer surface.
3. Inspect Proxmox task/job/event history for the build window.
4. Inspect NetBird overlay state for the newly built or modified resources.
5. Inspect Porkbun DNS/domain/SSL state only when the build changed or depends on public edge configuration.
6. Check application/service endpoints using GMRI engineering tools where appropriate.
7. Compare intended vs observed state.
8. Write an evidence-backed result as one of:
   - PASS
   - DEGRADED
   - FAIL
   - BLOCKED
9. Preserve exact receipts, timestamps, resource IDs, task IDs/UPIDs, peer IDs, DNS records, and unresolved discrepancies.

The builder does not certify itself.

## Authority model

Default unattended authority:

- OBSERVE
- RETRIEVE
- COMPARE
- REASON
- INVESTIGATE
- COLLECT EVIDENCE
- REPORT
- ALERT

Mutating infrastructure, network policy, DNS, SSL, domain registration, renewal, transfer, purchase, deletion, or credential changes require prior authority appropriate to the action.

Prefer bounded, reversible, idempotent changes. Never:

- grant the system additional authority to solve its own blocker;
- expose arbitrary public ports;
- weaken NetBird or firewall policy merely to make a test pass;
- alter credentials unnecessarily;
- silently overwrite a known-good deployment;
- delete evidence;
- make irreversible infrastructure changes without explicit authorization;
- purchase or renew domains unless that purchase authority was explicitly granted.

When blocked, record `BLOCKED_REQUIRES_OPERATOR` and continue safe independent work elsewhere.

## Evidence and rollback

Before mutation:

1. inspect;
2. record baseline;
3. identify authoritative state;
4. establish rollback/recovery path;
5. create or attach to durable run state;
6. only then mutate.

After mutation, verify the narrowest relevant area, then independently recon where practical. Preserve actor, authority, intended effect, observed result, and receipt.

## Routing with GMRI Engineering Operations

Use GMRI Cloud Access System for infrastructure, network-overlay, and public-edge concerns. Use GMRI Engineering Operations for repository/application engineering, host execution, build/test, and software-level acceptance. Combine them explicitly at the interface rather than collapsing infrastructure and application state into one layer.

Because I packaged a **legacy Codex compatibility manifest** into it, and that manifest declared an MCP server path through:

`"mcpServers": "./.mcp.json"`

That made ChatGPT/Codex treat part of the plugin as a **desktop/local-plugin style integration surface**, even though the actual Porkbun MCP is remote and the GMRI router itself should behave like the other account-saved plugins.

That was the wrong packaging choice.

I’ve already pushed two corrective revisions, but the plugin editor is preserving that legacy field in `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` because account-plugin updates are overlay-based and **cannot delete existing files/fields cleanly once they’re in the stored package**. So the current plugin identity is contaminated by the original packaging decision.

The clean fix is not another patch. It is to **recreate GMRI Cloud Access System as a fresh workspace plugin without the legacy `.codex-plugin` / `.mcp.json` compatibility layer at all**, using only:

- root `plugin.json`
- root `mcp.json` with Porkbun’s remote Streamable HTTP endpoint
- the GMRI Cloud Access System skill

That should make it behave like the other GMRI plugins and **not require desktop access**.

So yes: you’re right. It shouldn’t require desktop access, and the reason it does is the compatibility overlay I put in the first package.

[L2]   "content": "# Proxmox MCP Server\n\n> **NOTE:**\n> This project is under active development.\n\n## Motivation\n\nModern infrastructure often uses tools such as Terraform/OpenTofu, Ansible,\nand GitOps. These tools deploy and configure Proxmox infrastructure and\nKubernetes clusters.\n\nThe Proxmox MCP Server does not replace these tools. It gives AI assistants\nand automation agents access to information about your Proxmox clusters.\n\nThe default tools are read-only. Optional action tools can be enabled with\n`--allow-destructive` for operations such as backups and reboots.\n\nInstead of checking many pages in the Proxmox UI or running several commands,\nyou can ask an AI assistant to collect and analyze the required information.\nYour existing automation tools remain the main source for infrastructure\nchanges.\n\n## Overview\n\nThe server connects an MCP client, such as an AI assistant, to the Proxmox VE API.\nIt supports multiple Proxmox clusters and returns structured data.\n\nYou can use it to:\n\n- inspect clusters, nodes, and storage\n- check resource usage and node status\n- review recent Proxmox task events\n- find differences and possible configuration problems\n- collect information before you make infrastructure changes\n\nKeep your AI on the leash.\n\n## Proxmox core tools\n\nThe MCP server provides the following read-only tools:\n\n| Tool | Arguments | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `proxmox_clusters_list` | None | List the configured Proxmox clusters. |\n| `proxmox_clusters_describe` | `cluster` | Show a cluster's version, nodes, node statuses, and total resources. |\n| `proxmox_containers_list` | `cluster` | List LXC containers with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_containers_describe` | `cluster`, `vmid`, `node` (optional) | Show an LXC container's current status and runtime network interfaces when it is running. |\n| `proxmox_events_list` | `cluster`, `limit` (optional) | List recent task events across all nodes. The default limit is `10`. |\n| `proxmox_nodes_list` | `cluster` | List nodes with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_nodes_describe` | `cluster`, `node` | Show a node's status, resources, uptime, version, kernel, and boot information. |\n| `proxmox_storage_list` | `cluster` | List storage resources with their status, type, content, and capacity usage. |\n| `proxmox_storage_describe` | `cluster`, `name`, `node` (optional) | Show storage details and, when a node is provided, content visible on that node. |\n| `proxmox_vms_list` | `cluster` | List QEMU virtual machines with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_vms_describe` | `cluster`, `vmid`, `node` (optional) | Show a QEMU virtual machine's current status and guest network interfaces when its QEMU guest agent is responding. |\n\nUse `proxmox_clusters_list` first to find the cluster names used by the other\ntools. MCP clients can discover the full input and output schemas. You can\nalso list the tools from the command line:\n\n```sh\nproxmox-mcp tools --config /absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml\n```\n\nWhen `--allow-destructive` is enabled, `proxmox_vms_backup` and\n`proxmox_containers_backup` accept `cluster`, `vmid`, optional `node`,\n`storage`, `mode`, and `compress` arguments. They start an asynchronous backup\nand return its Proxmox task identifier; task creation does not mean that the\nbackup has already completed successfully.\n\n## Installation\n\nFor a local installation with Homebrew, run:\n\n```sh\nbrew install sergelogvinov/tap/proxmox-mcp\n```\n\nYou do not need a local installation when you use an MCP server hosted on\nanother machine.\n\n## Configure Proxmox clusters\n\nCreate a YAML file that contains one or more Proxmox clusters:\n\n```yaml\nclusters:\n  - region: homelab\n    url: https://pve.example.com:8006/api2/json\n    token_id: mcp@pve!reader\n    token_secret_file: /absolute/path/to/token-secret\n    ca_file: /absolute/path/to/proxmox-ca.crt\n```\n\nEach cluster supports these fields:\n\n| Field | Required | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `region` | Yes | Unique name used to select the cluster in tool calls. |\n| `url` | Yes | Full Proxmox API URL, including `/api2/json`. |\n| `token_id` | For token login | Proxmox API token ID, for example `mcp@pve!reader`. |\n| `token_id_file` | For token login | File that contains the token ID. Use this instead of `token_id`. |\n| `token_secret` | For token login | Proxmox API token secret. |\n| `token_secret_file` | For token login | File that contains the token secret. Use this instead of `token_secret`. |\n| `username` | For password login | Proxmox user name. Must be used with `password`. |\n| `password` | For password login | Proxmox password. Must be used with `username`. |\n| `ca_file` | No | Path to the CA certificate used to check the Proxmox TLS certificate. |\n| `insecure` | No | Skip TLS certificate checks. Use only for local testing. Default: `false`. |\n\nUse either token login or password login for a cluster, not both. Files are\nrecommended for secrets because they keep secret values out of the YAML file.\nThe Proxmox account should have only the permissions required by the tools.\n\nSet the configuration path with `--config` or `CONFIG_FILE`.\n\n## Configure an MCP client\n\n### Local stdio server\n\nFor clients that use a JSON MCP configuration, add an entry like this:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"proxmox\": {\n      \"command\": \"proxmox-mcp\",\n      \"args\": [\"mcp\"],\n      \"env\": {\n        \"CONFIG_FILE\": \"/absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml\"\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\n### Remote HTTP server\n\nStart the streamable HTTP server with:\n\n```sh\nproxmox-mcp server \\\n  --config /absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml \\\n  --listen-address :8080\n```\n\n`:8080` accepts connections on every IPv4 and IPv6 address. To listen on one\naddress, give it with the port, for example `127.0.0.1:8080` or `[::1]:8080`.\nThe MCP endpoint is `http://host:8080/mcp`\n\nFor a remote client, use an HTTPS URL that ends with `/mcp`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"proxmox\": {\n      \"type\": \"http\",\n      \"url\": \"https://proxmox-mcp.example.com/mcp\",\n      \"headers\": {\n        \"Authorization\": \"Bearer PVEAPIToken=mcp@pve!reader=TOKEN_SECRET\"\n      }\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nThe server does not provide user authentication for the HTTP endpoint.\nIt relies on Proxmox authentication and API tokens for access control.\nProvide the token in mcp header like:\n\n```text\nAuthorization: PVEAPIToken=mcp@pve!reader=TOKEN_SECRET\n```\n\nWhen this header is present, its token is used for the tool call instead of\nthe credentials from the cluster configuration. The configured cluster must\nstill include `region` and `url`.\n\nRestart or reload the MCP client after you save its configuration.\n\n## Running\n\n### Common flags\n\nThe `mcp`, `server`, and `tools` commands use the following flags. Each flag\ncan also be set with an environment variable. A command-line flag has higher\npriority than an environment variable.\n\n| Flag | Environment variable | Default | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `--config <path>` | `CONFIG_FILE` | None | Path to the required clusters YAML configuration file. |\n| `--extensions <list>` | `EXTENSIONS` | `all` | Comma-separated list of extensions to enable, or `all`. |\n| `--allow-destructive` | `ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE` | `false` | Allow destructive tools when they are available. Current core tools are read-only. |\n| `--log-level <level>` | `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | Log level: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, or `error`. |\n| `--log-format <format>` | `LOG_FORMAT` | `text` | Log output format: `text` or `json`. |\n\nThe `server` command also accepts `--listen-address` or `LISTEN_ADDRESS`\n(`host:port`). The default is `127.0.0.1:8080`, and the container image sets\n`LISTEN_ADDRESS=:8080`. The `tools` command accepts `--output` (`-o`) with `text`, `json`, or\n`yaml`. Its default is `text`.\n\nFor example, run the stdio server with JSON logs:\n\n```sh\nproxmox-mcp mcp \\\n  --config /absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml \\\n  --log-format json\n```\n\n## Test the configuration\n\nList all available tools:\n\n```sh\nexport CONFIG_FILE=\"/absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml\"\nproxmox-mcp tools\n```\n\nCall a tool directly:\n\n```sh\nproxmox-mcp tools proxmox_clusters_list\nproxmox-mcp tools proxmox_nodes_list cluster=homelab\nproxmox-mcp tools -o json proxmox_events_list cluster=homelab limit=5\n```\n\n## License\n\nLicensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the \"License\");\nyou may not use this file except in compliance with the License.\nYou may obtain a copy of the License at\n\n[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)\n\nUnless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing, software\ndistributed under the License is distributed on an \"AS IS\" BASIS,\nWITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied.\nSee the License for the specific language governing permissions and\nlimitations under the License.\n\n---\n\n`Proxmox®` is a registered trademark of [Proxmox Server Solutions GmbH](https://www.proxmox.com/en/about/company).\n",

Optional action tools can be enabled with\n`--allow-destructive` for operations such as backups and reboots.\n\nInstead of checking many pages in the Proxmox UI or running several commands,\nyou can ask an AI assistant to collect and analyze the required information.\nYour existing automation tools remain the main source for infrastructure\nchanges.\n\n## Overview\n\nThe server connects an MCP client, such as an AI assistant, to the Proxmox VE API.\nIt supports multiple Proxmox clusters and returns structured data.\n\nYou can use it to:\n\n- inspect clusters, nodes, and storage\n- check resource usage and node status\n- review recent Proxmox task events\n- find differences and possible configuration problems\n- collect information before you make infrastructure changes\n\nKeep your AI on the leash.\n\n## Proxmox core tools\n\nThe MCP server provides the following read-only tools:\n\n| Tool | Arguments | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `proxmox_clusters_list` | None | List the configured Proxmox clusters. |\n| `proxmox_clusters_describe` | `cluster` | Show a cluster's version, nodes, node statuses, and total resources. |\n| `proxmox_containers_list` | `cluster` | List LXC containers with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_containers_describe` | `cluster`, `vmid`, `node` (optional) | Show an LXC container's current status and runtime network interfaces when it is running. |\n| `proxmox_events_list` | `cluster`, `limit` (optional) | List recent task events across all nodes. The default limit is `10`. |\n| `proxmox_nodes_list` | `cluster` | List nodes with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_nodes_describe` | `cluster`, `node` | Show a node's status, resources, uptime, version, kernel, and boot information. |\n| `proxmox_storage_list` | `cluster` | List storage resources with their status, type, content, and capacity usage. |\n| `proxmox_storage_describe` | `cluster`, `name`, `node` (optional) | Show storage details and, when a node is provided, content visible on that node. |\n| `proxmox_vms_list` | `cluster` | List QEMU virtual machines with their status and resource usage. |\n| `proxmox_vms_describe` | `cluster`, `vmid`, `node` (optional) | Show a QEMU virtual machine's current status and guest network interfaces when its QEMU guest agent is responding. |\n\nUse `proxmox_clusters_list` first to find the cluster names used by the other\ntools. MCP clients can discover the full input and output schemas. You can\nalso list the tools from the command line:\n\n```sh\nproxmox-mcp tools --config /absolute/path/to/cluster-config.yaml\n```\n\nWhen `--allow-destructive` is enabled, `proxmox_vms_backup` and\n`proxmox_containers_backup` accept `cluster`, `vmid`, optional `node`,\n`storage`, `mode`, and `compress` arguments. They start an asynchronous backup\nand return its Proxmox task identifier; task creation does not mean that the\nbackup has already completed successfully.\n\n## Installation\n\nFor a local installation with Homebrew, run:\n\n```sh\nbrew install sergelogvinov/tap/proxmox-mcp\n```\n\nYou do not need a local installation when you use an MCP server hosted on\nanother machine.\n\n## Configure Proxmox clusters\n\nCreate a YAML file that contains one or more Proxmox clusters:\n\n```yaml\nclusters:\n  - region: homelab\n    url: https://pve.example.com:8006/api2/json\n    token_id: mcp@pve!reader\n    token_secret_file: /absolute/path/to/token-secret\n    ca_file: /absolute/path/to/proxmox-ca.crt\n```\n\nEach cluster supports these fields:\n\n| Field | Required | Description |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `region` | Yes | Unique name used to select the cluster in tool calls. |\n| `url` | Yes | Full Proxmox API URL, including `/api2/json`. |\n| `token_id` | For token login | Proxmox API token ID, for example `mcp@pve!reader`. |\n| `token_id_file` | For token login | File that contains the token ID. Use this instead of `token_id`. |\n| `token_secret` | For token login | Proxmox API token secret. |\n| `token_secret_file` | For token login | File that contains the token secret. Use this instead of `token_secret`. |\n| `username` | For password login | Proxmox user name. Must be used with `password`. |\n| `password` | For password login | Proxmox password. Must be used with `username`. |\n| `ca_file` | No | Path to the CA certificate used to check the Proxmox TLS certificate. |\n| `insecure` | No | Skip TLS certificate checks. Use only for local testing. Default: `false`. |\n\nUse either token login or password login for a cluster, not both. Files are\nrecommended for secrets because they keep secret values out of the YAML file.\nThe Proxmox account should have only the permissions required by the tools.\n\nSet the configuration path with `--config` or `CONFIG_FILE`.\n\n## Configure an MCP client\n\n### Local stdio server\n\nFor clients that use a JSON MCP configuration, add an entry like this:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcpServers\": {\n    \"proxmox\": {\n      \"command\": \"proxmox-mcp\",\n      \"args\": [\"mcp\"... architecture](docs/assets/proxmoxmcp-nature-architecture.svg)\n\n## Why ProxmoxMCP-Plus\n\nProxmoxMCP-Plus sits between AI clients and Proxmox VE so operators do not have to stitch together raw API calls, one-off shell scripts, and custom job polling for every workflow.\n\nIt exposes the same operational surface in two ways:\n\n- `MCP` for Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Open WebUI, Codex, and other MCP-capable agents\n- `OpenAPI` for HTTP automation, dashboards, internal tools, and no-code workflows\n\nWhat you get:\n\n- VM and LXC lifecycle actions\n- snapshot create, rollback, and delete\n- backup and restore workflows\n- ISO download and cleanup\n- node, storage, and cluster inspection\n- SSH-backed container command execution with guardrails\n- persistent job tracking for async Proxmox tasks\n\n## What Makes It Different\n\n| Priority | How the project handles it |\n| --- | --- |\n| Dual access paths | Native MCP for agent workflows and OpenAPI for standard HTTP automation |\n| Proxmox-oriented workflows | Day-2 VM, LXC, snapshot, backup, ISO, storage, and cluster operations |\n| Long-running operations | Stable `job_id`s, Proxmox `UPID` tracking, polling, retry, cancel, and audit history |\n| Safer execution | Proxmox API tokens, OpenAPI bearer auth, command policy, approval tokens, TLS validation, and MCP HTTP Host/Origin controls |\n| Real validation | Unit, integration, Docker/OpenAPI, and live Proxmox e2e entry points are documented in the repo |\n\n## Quick Start\n\n### 1. Prepare Proxmox Credentials\n\nCreate a Proxmox API token with only the permissions your workflows need. Then create the local config file:\n\n```bash\ncp proxmox-config/config.example.json proxmox-config/config.json\n```\n\nThen edit `proxmox-config/config.json` with your environment. At minimum, it needs:\n\n- `proxmox.host`\n- `proxmox.port`\n- `auth.user`\n- `auth.token_name`\n- `auth.token_value`\n\nAdd an `ssh` section as well if you want container command execution.\nAdd a `jobs` section if you want job state persisted somewhere other than the default local SQLite file.\n\nFor real live verification, use a separate `proxmox-config/config.live.json` created from `proxmox-config/config.live.example.json`.\nDo not point live e2e at a placeholder or local-only `config.json` unless you intentionally run a local API tunnel there.\n\nOptional job persistence config:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"jobs\": {\n    \"sqlite_path\": \"proxmox-jobs.sqlite3\"\n  }\n}\n```\n\nOptional tool exposure filtering can reduce the schemas sent to MCP clients. It is\ndisabled by default, so existing configurations continue to expose every available\ntool. Configure exactly one mode under `mcp`:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"mcp\": {\n    \"tool_allowlist\": [\"get_nodes\", \"get_vms\", \"get_containers\", \"get_storage\"]\n  }\n}\n```\n\nAlternatively, use `tool_denylist`, or the comma-separated environment variables\n`MCP_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` and `MCP_TOOL_DENYLIST`. Do not configure both modes. Environment\nselection replaces the file-level filtering mode. An empty allowlist exposes no tools;\nan empty denylist hides none. Exact lowercase tool names are required, and unknown names\nfail startup so a typo cannot silently widen access. Restart or reconnect the MCP server\nafter changing the filter.\n\n### 2. Choose One Runtime Path\n\n| Path | Best for | Start command | Verify |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| MCP stdio from PyPI | Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, local agents | `uvx proxmox-mcp-plus` | client lists `get_nodes`, `get_vms`, and job tools |\n| Native MCP HTTP from Docker | remote MCP clients that support Streamable HTTP | `docker compose --profile mcp-http up -d proxmox-mcp-http` | connect to `http://localhost:8000/mcp` |\n| OpenAPI bridge from Docker | HTTP clients, dashboards, scripts, no-code tools | `docker compose up -d` | `curl -f http://localhost:8811/livez` |\n\n#### MCP stdio with PyPI\n\n```bash\nuvx proxmox-mcp-plus\n```\n\nOr install it first:\n\n```bash\npip install proxmox-mcp-plus\nproxmox-mcp-plus\n```\n\nUse this path when the MCP client launches a local stdio server.\n\n#### Code Mode (opt-in)\n\nCode Mode is disabled by default to preserve the legacy full tool catalog. Enable it\nwith `mcp.code_mode: true` in the config file or `MCP_CODE_MODE=true`. When enabled,\nMCP exposes three tools instead: `proxmox_code_search`, `proxmox_code_get_schema`, and\n`proxmox_code_execute`. Code execution runs in an isolated sandbox and reaches domain\ntools through the existing validation, policy, and approval path. Discovery uses the\nfiltered runtime catalog, so it also works in installed wheels. For example:\n\n```python\nawait call_tool(\"get_nodes\", {\"target\": \"default\"})\n```\n\nThe final expression is returned as `data.result`; tool results use MCP JSON content\nblocks (and structured content where supplied). Use `proxmox_code_get_schema` for\narguments, including `target` and approval tokens. Scripts have no filesystem or\nnetwork access except registered tool calls. Limits: 64,000 source characters,\n100 MB sandbox memory, 25 tool calls, 16 KB final JSON, and two concurrent executions.\nExecution has a 30-second budget; cancelling or failing a script does not roll back\ntool side effects. Do not automatically retry a failed mutation script.\n\nOptional worker reuse: set `mcp.code_mode_pool_reuse: true` or\n`MCP_CODE_MODE_POOL_REUSE=true`. The default remains one fresh worker per execution.\nReuse keeps up to two workers for the server lifetime, recycles each after 100\ncheckouts, and starts a new sandbox session per request. Globals, approvals, output\ncollectors and call limits are not shared between requests. HTTP clients share the\nserver-owned pool; disconnecting a client does not close it. Run\n`python scripts/benchmark_code_mode.py` to measure local startup overhead; this is\na microbenchmark, not an estimate of Proxmox operation latency.\n\n\n#### Native MCP HTTP with Docker\n\nUse this path when a remote MCP client supports Streamable HTTP:\n\n```bash\nexport MCP_API_KEY=\"$(openssl rand -hex 32)\"\ndocker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \\\n  -e PROXMOX_MCP_MODE=mcp-http \\\n  -e MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0 \\\n  -e MCP_PORT=8000 \\\n  -e MCP_TRANSPORT=STREAMABLE_HTTP \\\n  -e MCP_API_KEY=\"$MCP_API_KEY\" \\\n  -v \"$(pwd)/proxmox-config/config.json:/app/proxmox-config/config.json:ro\" \\\n  ghcr.io/rekklesna/proxmoxmcp-plus:latest\n```\n\nPoint MCP clients at:\n\n```text\nhttp://<docker-host>:8000/mcp\n```\n\nSend `Authorization: Bearer <MCP_API_KEY>` with every native MCP HTTP request.\nThe key is independent of Proxmox credentials. Native Streamable HTTP and SSE\nrequire a key by default. For an endpoint protected by an external access-control\nlayer such as Tailscale ACLs, explicitly set `MCP_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED_HTTP=true`\nor `mcp.allow_unauthenticated_http: true` in JSON configuration. This allows\nkeyless startup and logs a warning; it does not configure or verify the external\naccess controls. A configured `MCP_API_KEY` is always enforced, even with opt-out.\nThis setting does not change OpenAPI authentication or DNS rebinding protection.\n\n##### OAuth browser gate for MCP clients\n\nNative MCP HTTP can optionally expose an OAuth authorization-code flow with PKCE\nwhile keeping `MCP_API_KEY` as the only human credential an operator has to\nmanage. OAuth protocol handling is delegated to the MCP Python SDK\n(`mcp>=1.30.0,<2`), while ProxmoxMCP-Plus provides the API-key consent policy\nand persistent OAuth state.\n\nOAuth state is stored in PostgreSQL. This allows multiple MCP server instances or\nhosts, when deployed explicitly, to share registered clients, authorization codes,\naccess tokens, refresh tokens, refresh-token replay protection, and login-rate-limit\nstate without relying on a local filesystem.\n\nThe client starts at the SDK `/authorize` endpoint. After the SDK validates the\nclient, redirect URI, scope, PKCE request, and resource, the browser is redirected\nto `/oauth/consent` on the same MCP origin. The user reviews the client name,\nredirect origin, and requested scopes, then enters `MCP_API_KEY`. The API key is\nnever placed in a URL and is never returned to the OAuth client.\n\nRequired OAuth settings:\n\n```bash\nexport MCP_API_KEY=\"$(openssl rand -hex 32)\"\nexport MCP_OAUTH_DATABASE_URL='postgresql://proxmox_oauth:secret@postgres.example:5432/proxmox_oauth'\n```\n\nExample server:\n\n```bash\ndocker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \\\n  -e PROXMOX_MCP_MODE=mcp-http \\\n  -e MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0 \\\n  -e MCP_PORT=8000 \\\n  -e MCP_TRANSPORT=STREAMABLE_HTTP \\\n  -e MCP_API_KEY=\"$MCP_API_KEY\" \\\n  -e MCP_OAUTH_ENABLED=true \\\n  -e MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER=https://mcp.example.com \\\n  -e MCP_OAUTH_DATABASE_URL=\"$MCP_OAUTH_DATABASE_URL\" \\\n  -e MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS=mcp.example.com:*,localhost:* \\\n  -e MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://mcp.example.com \\\n  -v \"$(pwd)/proxmox-config/config.json:/app/proxmox-config/config.json:ro\" \\\n  ghcr.io/rekklesna/proxmoxmcp-plus:latest\n```\n\nThen connect the OAuth-capable client to:\n\n```text\nhttps://mcp.example.com/mcp\n```\n\nOAuth mode exposes these endpoints on the same public origin:\n\n- `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp` - RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata\n- `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` - SDK authorization-server metadata\n- `/register` - SDK dynamic client registration (DCR)\n- `/authorize` - SDK authorization endpoint\n- `/token` - SDK authorization-code/refresh-token exchange\n- `/oauth/consent` - ProxmoxMCP-Plus API-key consent page\n\nThe SDK requires PKCE `S256` and protects the MCP resource with issued OAuth\naccess tokens. Browser consent transactions are short-lived, HMAC-signed, and\nstateless. All durable OAuth state is stored in PostgreSQL.\n\nAuthorization-code consumption and refresh-token rotation use PostgreSQL\ntransactions. A code or refresh token is deleted and its replacement tokens are\ninserted atomically, so concurrent server instances cannot successfully replay the\nsame credential. Dynamic client registration capacity is also serialized with a\nPostgreSQL transaction-scoped advisory lock; inactive registrations are pruned\nbefore the configured limit is exceeded.\n\n`MCP_API_KEY` is the sole source of truth for the browser consent credential.\nThis runtime does not persist the key or its verifier in PostgreSQL. The server process\nvalidates consent directly against the value supplied in its environment. If the\nservice is explicitly deployed as multiple containers or instances, configure the\nsame secret for each instance. Stop all instances before changing the key, then\nrestart/recreate all of them with the new value before routing traffic again.\nExisting OAuth clients and issued tokens are independent of the browser-gate key\nand remain valid until they expire or are revoked.\n\nRequired when OAuth is enabled:\n\n| Variable | Purpose |\n| --- | --- |\n| `MCP_API_KEY` | Human credential entered only on the consent page |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER` | Public HTTPS origin of this MCP authorization server |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_DATABASE_URL` | PostgreSQL DSN used for OAuth state |\n\nOptional OAuth environment variables:\n\n| Variable | Default | Purpose |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_RESOURCE` | `<issuer>/mcp` | Public MCP resource identifier; must use the issuer origin |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_SCOPES` | `mcp` | Comma-separated required scopes |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS` | `3600` | Access-token lifetime |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS` | `2592000` | Refresh-token lifetime (30 days) |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_MAX_REGISTERED_CLIENTS` | `4096` | Maximum persisted DCR clients before inactive-client pruning |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_DB_POOL_MIN_SIZE` | `1` | Minimum asyncpg connections per MCP process |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_DB_POOL_MAX_SIZE` | `10` | Maximum asyncpg connections per MCP process |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_DB_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `10` | PostgreSQL command timeout used by the OAuth store |\n| `MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` | unset | Trusted reverse-proxy header used only for login rate limiting |\n\nTo rotate the browser-gate credential, stop every MCP instance using this issuer,\nupdate `MCP_API_KEY` in the deployment environment, and restart/recreate all\ninstances with the same new key. The environment is read when the provider starts;\nediting a running container's environment does not reload its key. No OAuth\ndatabase metadata or key-version update is required. Pending consent transactions\ncreated with the previous key will no longer validate after every instance has\nrestarted; already issued OAuth tokens remain governed by their normal lifetime\nand revocation rules. A rolling key change leaves old instances accepting the old\nkey and causes consent requests routed between different-key instances to fail.\nThere is no database guard to detect or disable a stale instance. Changing the\nbrowser-gate key does not revoke existing access tokens, refresh tokens, or\nauthorization codes; use explicit revocation for compromised OAuth credentials.\n\nWhen upgrading from an OAuth build that used `MCP_OAUTH_KEY_VERSION`, startup\nignores the old variable and leaves `proxmox_mcp_oauth_metadata` untouched. Fresh\ndatabases do not create that table. Registered clients and issued OAuth credentials\nare preserved; no manual SQL migration is required. Keeping legacy metadata avoids\nbreaking old workers' queries and permits rollback with the same API key and\nlegacy key version. Back up the database before upgrading and stop all old\ninstances before rotating the key. After a key change, the legacy metadata still\ndescribes the old key: rollback requires restoring the old configuration or\nfollowing the old version's rotation procedure, which invalidates OAuth state.\nOnly remove the legacy table manually once all old instances are retired and a\nrollback is no longer needed; it can still contain the previous key's verifier.\... name: gmri-proxmox-control

# GMRI Proxmox Control

Use this skill as GMRI's Proxmox control and verification router.

## Two-lane architecture

Treat the two MCPs as complementary, not redundant.

### Operator lane — ProxmoxMCP-Plus

Repository: `RekklesNA/ProxmoxMCP-Plus`

Use for deliberate operator-authorized work such as:
- VM and LXC lifecycle operations;
- resource creation and configuration;
- snapshots, rollback, backup, and restore workflows;
- storage and ISO operations;
- persistent asynchronous job tracking;
- stable `job_id` and Proxmox UPID receipts;
- tool allowlist/denylist scoping;
- approval-token guarded dangerous actions;
- remote Streamable HTTP or local stdio deployment.

Prefer Proxmox API tokens with least privilege. Preserve TLS verification. Keep dangerous operations behind explicit approval/authority boundaries.

### Observer lane — sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp

Repository: `sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp`

Use as the independent read-side verifier for:
- cluster inventory;
- node status and resource usage;
- VM and LXC status;
- storage state;
- recent Proxmox task events;
- discrepancy/configuration review;
- pre-change and post-change observation.

Keep destructive mode disabled for ordinary recon. The builder/operator should not certify itself when this independent observer path is available.

## OminPi / Oh My Pi handoff contract

When this skill is used to prepare instructions for an OminPi/Oh My Pi engineering agent, the handoff must be executable without chat history.

The handoff must contain:

1. mission objective;
2. known-good baseline requirements;
3. exact target environment and source-of-truth references;
4. required MCP installation/configuration steps;
5. credential handling rules;
6. authority envelope;
7. resource inventory to inspect before mutation;
8. intended resource blueprint;
9. staged implementation order;
10. verification steps after each stage;
11. rollback/recovery steps;
12. durable run-state/evidence requirements;
13. acceptance gates;
14. blocked-state behavior;
15. final operator handoff.

Do not stop at architecture prose. Produce commands/config templates/checklists where source evidence supports them.

## Installation guidance for OminPi agent

### ProxmoxMCP-Plus

Preferred remote-agent deployment when the OminPi agent needs broad operator capability:
- deploy the native MCP HTTP service in Docker or another controlled runtime;
- use Streamable HTTP;
- require `MCP_API_KEY` or OAuth; do not disable MCP authentication merely because an encrypted overlay is present;
- bind only to the intended interface or place it behind the approved overlay/reverse proxy;
- use `MCP_TOOL_ALLOWLIST` or config allowlist to expose only required tools;
- use Proxmox API token credentials with least privilege;
- keep TLS verification enabled;
- persist job state to the configured SQLite or PostgreSQL-backed components as appropriate to the chosen mode;
- do not place secrets in Git, chat, drop packets, or plaintext evidence logs.

For local stdio clients, `uvx proxmox-mcp-plus` is a supported path. For remote MCP, the repository documents native Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`.

### Independent observer

Install `sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp` separately from the operator surface when practical.

Supported patterns include:
- Homebrew/local install for a host-side observer;
- remote Streamable HTTP server ending in `/mcp`;
- token-secret files rather than inline secrets;
- one or more named clusters in YAML configuration.

Keep this lane read-only by default.

## Resource blueprinting workflow

Before creating or restructuring Proxmox resources:

1. enumerate cluster(s), node(s), storage pools, bridges/VLANs, existing VMs/LXCs, templates, backup targets, and current task/event state;
2. record versions, capacities, free space, current CPU/RAM pressure, storage content types, network assumptions, and naming/ID collisions;
3. identify which existing resources are canonical, transitional, disposable, or unknown;
4. separate desired-state design from observed-state evidence;
5. write a proposed resource map before mutation;
6. assign IDs, names, roles, CPU/RAM/storage/network requirements, persistence class, backup policy, recovery priority, and authority owner for each resource;
7. define build order based on dependency graph;
8. establish rollback before each mutation;
9. mutate through the operator lane;
10. verify through the observer lane where possible;
11. reconcile intended vs observed state and record discrepancies.

## Post-build recon

For an Oh My Pi/OpenRig build completion event:

1. read durable build receipt and run ID;
2. read intended state and acceptance criteria;
3. inspect actual Proxmox state via independent observer;
4. inspect task/event history for the build window;
5. compare resource IDs, names, power state, assigned CPU/RAM, storage, network-visible state, and relevant guest-agent data;
6. check backups/snapshots if acceptance requires them;
7. classify result as `PASS`, `DEGRADED`, `FAIL`, or `BLOCKED`;
8. preserve exact evidence and unresolved discrepancies.

## Authority model

Default unattended authority:
- OBSERVE
- RETRIEVE
- COMPARE
- REASON
- INVESTIGATE
- COLLECT EVIDENCE
- REPORT
- ALERT

Mutation requires prior authority appropriate to the exact action. Prefer bounded, reversible, idempotent changes.

Never:
- grant the agent broader Proxmox privileges to solve its own blocker;
- switch off TLS verification merely to make a connection work;
- expose an MCP endpoint publicly without an explicit network/security decision;
- store Proxmox token secrets in the plugin package;
- retry an uncertain mutation blindly;
- delete evidence or rollback material;
- overwrite known-good resources without a verified recovery path.

When blocked, record `BLOCKED_REQUIRES_OPERATOR` and continue safe work elsewhere.

## Evidence model

Before mutation:
- inspect;
- baseline;
- identify authority/source of truth;
- establish rollback;
- attach to durable run state;
- only then mutate.

For consequential actions preserve:
- actor;
- authority;
- target resource;
- intended effect;
- command/tool call reference;
- job ID/UPID if available;
- observed result;
- independent verification result;
- rollback reference.

## Output expectations

When asked for a drop-off packet or OminPi handoff, provide a self-contained engineering handoff, not a conversational summary. Unknown environment-specific values must be explicit placeholders or `UNRESOLVED` items, never invented.

[L63]  ### RELEASE CONTROL

[L65]  Use this audit revision in place of earlier v1.2 copies. The required outcome remains both the
[L66]  trusted-network GEV service and the iMac built-in panel. A working web page alone is not
[L67]  completion. See Section 13 for acceptance states and Section 17 for execution order.

[L69]  1. Mission

[L71]  Deploy the GMRI fork of God's Eye View into a dedicated Proxmox VE 9 LXC on the 2017 iMac host at
[L72]  100.98.1.114. Expose the Radeon Pro 570 through native dev[n] device passthrough, and drive the
[L73]  otherwise-unused built-in 5K panel with a hardware-accelerated kiosk browser inside that LXC.
[L74]  Keep the same GEV service reachable from the trusted network. Preserve GEV as the GMRI
[L75]  macro-scale geospatial plane; this job does not implement or replace the Apple spatial clients,
[L76]  Project Sovereign, or the reconstruction pipeline. [R1, R2]

[L78]  ▏ Execution rule | Proceed end-to-end while the operator is away. Discover live state; make
[L79]  ▏ routine reversible decisions; retain command output and rollback points. Do not request routine
[L80]  ▏ choices. A genuine access, capacity, hardware, or security blocker must produce a BLOCKED or
[L81]  ▏ PARTIAL receipt, not an invented success or an unbounded retry loop.

[L83]  Command locations: HOST means the Proxmox host reached through the existing authorized management
[L84]  path; CT means root inside the selected container via pct exec; GEV means the non-root gev
[L85]  account inside that container; AGENT means the local deployment workstation. Do not install Node,
[L86]  Chromium, or a desktop environment on the Proxmox host. Samples with shell variables require
[L87]  agent-resolved, validated values, not operator input.

[L89]  2. Target environment

[L120]  3. Source of truth and deployment baseline

[L122]  Origin must be https://github.com/oldmangrizzz/gods-eye-view.git; upstream is
[L123]  https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git for provenance only. The inspected main commit
[L124]  is b74a0233d9b94bd48329e60009d3877532e04ab2 (05 October 2026). At execution start, resolve
[L125]  origin/main once, record that SHA, and freeze the candidate to it for the entire run. Do not
[L126]  auto-merge upstream or keep pulling a moving main while testing. [R3]

[L128]  Section 9 creates a separate candidate release. Never clone into, reset, or replace an existing
[L129]  active checkout without first identifying and preserving it. Reuse a previously created GEV
[L130]  container only when the deployment manifest proves it belongs to this assignment; otherwise
[L131]  select a fresh CTID.

[L133]  The inspected package requires Node >=24.14.0 <25 or >=26 <27. Install dependencies with npm ci
[L134]  --include=dev: Vite and other required runtime/testing packages are in devDependencies. Use the
[L135]  repository-supported local-provider server, not static dist hosting alone. Preserve the package
[L136]  lockfile. [R3]

[L138]  4. Desired end state

[L140]  - GEV runs as the non-root gev service account inside a dedicated LXC; neither npm install
[L141]    scripts nor the web service run as root.
[L142]  - The LXC starts automatically after acceptance. A DHCP reservation or verified existing
[L143]    allocation provides a stable address; a dynamic lease alone is reported as lease-only, not a
[L144]    guaranteed stable address.
[L145]  - The Radeon Pro 570 DRM card and render node are passed into the LXC through Proxmox VE 9 dev[n]
[L146]    device passthrough.
[L147]  - The GPU identity, internal panel EDID/connector, active CRTC, and selected mode are recorded.
[L148]    Prefer the actual advertised 5120x2880 mode; any lower resolution is a declared degraded
[L149]    result.
[L150]  - A dedicated Xorg server controls the selected AMD KMS device and reserved host VT; Chromium
[L151]    runs as gevdisplay on that real X display against http://127.0.0.1:4173. A small window manager
[L152]    may provide reliable kiosk/fullscreen behavior.
[L153]  - The display does not sleep or blank during normal operation.
[L154]  - GEV remains independently usable from another LAN browser even if the physical kiosk session is
[L155]    stopped.
[L156]  - No provider secret is committed to Git or baked into the browser bundle except keys explicitly
[L157]    designed to be client-visible by GEV.
[L158]  - The receipt records A1-A18 individually, including command exit codes, exact versions,
[L159]    ownership, network exposure, mode, renderer, sandbox evidence, changes, and rollback. A
[L160]    requirement is not a test result.

[L162]  5. Host discovery gate

[L164]  HOST / AGENT - Establish the already-authorized SSH/overlay route and host identity before
[L165]  writing. Record existing guests, service ownership, storage health, firewall state, and a working
[L166]  management session. Discover GPU PCI identity and its actual card/render nodes; do not infer them
[L167]  from numbering. Treat missing diagnostic utilities as missing observations, not successful
[L168]  checks.

[L170]  ```text
[L171]    pveversion -v
[L172]    hostnamectl
[L173]    cat /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name
   lscpu
[L175]    free -h
[L176]    swapon --show
[L177]    lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
[L178]    findmnt
[L179]    pvesm status
[L180]    pct list
[L181]    qm list
[L182]    ip -br address
[L183]    ip -br link
[L184]    ip route show table all
[L185]    pveam available
[L186]    lspci -nnk
[L187]    ls -l /dev/dri /dev/dri/by-path
[L188]    for f in /sys/class/drm/card*-*/status; do
[L189]      [ -f "$f" ] || continue
[L190]      printf '%s: ' "$f"; cat "$f"
   done
 ```

[L194]  Record /sys/class/drm mappings, PCI driver, connector modes and EDID, plus current DRM users
[L195]  where fuser or lsof is available. Query actual pool health and free capacity using the installed
[L196]  storage tools. Prove that the card and render node belong to the same Radeon and identify the
[L197]  built-in panel, not merely any connected output. Failure of the graphics gate blocks display
[L198]  changes, not collection of evidence or preservation of a working GEV service.

[L200]  6. LXC creation baseline

[L202]  Start with an unprivileged Debian 13 amd64 system container. Debian 12 is an available-template
[L203]  fallback only after checking its packages meet the same acceptance gates. The narrowly scoped
[L204]  privileged fallback is defined in Section 14; never change an existing rootfs UID mapping by
[L205]  flipping a config flag.

[L207]  Baseline: 2 cores, cpulimit=2, 6144 MiB RAM, 2048 MiB swap allowance, 32 GiB root disk. Preserve
[L208]  at least 8 GiB of host RAM headroom after accounting for other guests; the agent may increase
[L209]  this CT to 3 cores / 8192 MiB only if measured kiosk load and host headroom justify it. Do not
[L210]  change host swap, storage layout, kernel, or other guests. Enable onboot only after the startup
[L211]  and identity guards are installed.

[L213]  HOST - Resolve CTID from the cluster-wide free-ID service and recheck immediately before
[L214]  creation. Choose template storage with vztmpl support and root storage with rootdir support;
[L215]  download an official template only if required. NETSPEC is the complete validated veth
[L216]  definition. For DHCP, omit gw entirely; for static addressing, require an existing authorized
[L217]  allocation, not an unused-looking address.

[L219]  ```text
[L220]    : "${CTID:?agent-resolved free ID required}"
[L221]    : "${TEMPLATE:?cached template volume required}"
[L222]    : "${STORAGE:?healthy rootdir storage required}"
[L223]    : "${NETSPEC:?validated network definition required}"
[L224]    pct create "$CTID" "$TEMPLATE" \
[L225]      --hostname gev --arch amd64 --ostype debian \
[L226]      --unprivileged 1 --cores 2 --cpulimit 2 \
[L227]      --memory 6144 --swap 2048 \
[L228]      --rootfs "${STORAGE}:32" --net0 "$NETSPEC" \
[L229]      --features nesting=0 --onboot 0 \
[L230]      --startup order=30,up=15,down=30
[L231]    pct start "$CTID"
 ```

[L234]  Do not include an empty gw= argument. Add VLAN, MTU, DNS and firewall options only from actual
[L235]  network configuration. Keep container SSH closed unless explicitly needed: pct exec provides
[L236]  administration. Test DNS, package access and the return route before installing the application.

[L238]  7. GPU and DRM passthrough - Proxmox VE 9

[L240]  HOST - Use Proxmox VE 9 native dev[n] passthrough for both the primary DRM node and its matching
[L241]  render node. Keep amdgpu bound on the host. A render node alone cannot perform modesetting; a
[L242]  connected connector query alone does not prove display ownership. Confirm the installed pct
[L243]  help/schema before applying options. [R4, R5]

[L245]  Create/query video and render groups inside the CT first. Resolve their container GIDs, select
[L246]  unused dev slots, stop only this CT, and apply the mappings. GPU_CARD and GPU_RENDER must come
[L247]  from the recorded Radeon PCI identity. These are container ownership values; do not chmod host
[L248]  devices to 0666 or give the web-service account GPU access.

[L250]  ```text
[L251]    : "${GPU_CARD:?resolved Radeon primary node required}"
[L252]    : "${GPU_RENDER:?resolved Radeon render node required}"
[L253]    : "${VIDEO_GID:?container video GID required}"
[L254]    : "${RENDER_GID:?container render GID required}"
[L255]    : "${CARD_SLOT:?unused dev slot required}"
[L256]    : "${RENDER_SLOT:?unused dev slot required}"
[L257]    pct shutdown "$CTID" --timeout 60
[L258]    pct set "$CTID" "--dev${CARD_SLOT}"

No apology needed. This is exactly the kind of evidence we should incorporate **before** turning an unattended build loose.

I went through both examples. They give us something much better than another abstract instruction: a **positive control and a negative control for agentic engineering behavior**.

The good GEV deployment had the right bones. It established a run ID and durable state before consequential work, initialized acceptance gates as `NOT RUN`, checkpointed before lifecycle/GPU/firewall/promotion operations, held a mutation lock, re-inspected live state instead of trusting planning observations, and treated “live state wins” as a rule. fileciteturn19file4 The underlying deployment PRD also explicitly says unattended execution means routine reversible decisions are delegated, while genuine blockers produce `BLOCKED` or `PARTIAL` rather than invented success or endless retries. fileciteturn17file1L57-L80

The shit-show gives us remarkably useful failure telemetry. It wasn't fundamentally a difficult-Proxmox problem. It was a **control-loop failure**. The agent used the wrong SSH identity, failed to consume supplied documentation, remained in Plan Mode while repeatedly designing mutations it could not perform, bounced among multiple file-transfer strategies after the environment had already told it writes were prohibited, hit a predictable Bun `${...}` interpolation problem, repeatedly reconsidered decisions it had already made, and spent cycles modeling *you* instead of the system. fileciteturn19file1 fileciteturn19file2 Worse, its own advisor eventually identified that the proposed ProxmoxMCP-Plus allowlist contained nonexistent tool names that would have caused the service to crash-loop—meaning execution readiness had not actually been established before it started trying to deploy. fileciteturn19file9

That changes my prompt in an important way. We need to make **agent-process integrity itself an acceptance gate**.

Use this version when you turn me loose:

> **GMRI OVERNIGHT ENGINEERING OPERATION — OMP/OPENRIG DROP-PACKET BUILD**
>
> You are the primary engineering coordinator for the GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute overnight build operation.

>

> Governing principle:

> **RELIEF OF WATCH WITHOUT ABANDONMENT OF WATCH.**
>
> ---
>
> ### 1. OPERATING DOCTRINE
>
> **Receipts before conclusions.  
> Live state before assumptions.  
> Code before prose.  
> Durable state before conversational state.  
> Recovery before mutation.  
> Independent verification before completion.**
>
> Never confuse:
>
> - a plan with execution;
> - an attempted command with an executed command;
> - HTTP response with application acceptance;
> - a green unit test with system acceptance;
> - documentation with implementation;
> - implementation with verification;
> - model reasoning with observed state;
> - inability to mutate with permission to continue designing mutations as though they occurred.
>
> Every consequential assertion must be classifiable as:
>
> `OBSERVED / SOURCE-SUPPORTED / TESTED / INFERRED / UNRESOLVED`
>
> Every implementation state must be classifiable as:
>
> `REAL-EXECUTABLE / TESTED-BUT-NARROW / IMPLEMENTED-NOT-VERIFIED / SCAFFOLD / DOCUMENTED-NOT-IMPLEMENTED / OVERCLAIMED / UNKNOWN`
>
> Ask continuously:
>
> **What proposition does this evidence actually establish?**
>
> ---

> ### 2. AGENT-PROCESS INTEGRITY GATE
>
> Before beginning implementation, prove that the execution environment can actually perform the intended work.
>
> Determine and record:
>
> - current execution mode;
> - read/write capability;
> - repository/worktree state;
> - actual available tools;
> - actual installed tool versions;
> - authentication state without exposing credentials;
> - reachable machines/services;
> - authoritative instruction files;
> - applicable authority boundaries.
>
> **If the environment is in Plan Mode or otherwise read-only, do not repeatedly design or attempt mutations.**
>
> Resolve the execution-state transition once. If that requires operator authorization, emit one precise `BLOCKED_REQUIRES_OPERATOR` receipt identifying the single required action. Continue independent safe/read-only work where useful.
>
> Do not spend cycles searching for alternate mutation mechanisms merely to bypass an intentional execution restriction.
>
> Never infer tool names, CLI syntax, APIs, flags, paths, usernames, schemas, or installed versions when they can be inspected.
>

>

>
> A proposed service configuration containing nonexistent tools, unsupported flags, invalid schema, or unverified version-specific syntax **fails preflight and may not advance to deployment**.
>
> ---
>
> ### 3. ANTI-THRASH / BOUNDED-RECOVERY RULE
>
> A failed operation must generate evidence before another attempt.
>
> For each failure:
>
> 1. capture exact operation and exit/error;
> 2. identify a specific falsifiable cause;
> 3. change one relevant variable;
> 4. record what changed;
> 5. retry.
>
> **Never repeat substantially identical failed operations without new evidence.**
>
> Maximum three attempts per identified recoverable cause unless new evidence materially changes the diagnosis.
>
> If three evidence-driven attempts fail:
>
> `BLOCKED`, `PARTIAL`, or `DEGRADED` as appropriate.
>
> Preserve the evidence and continue independent work elsewhere.
>
> Do not enter tool-selection loops such as:
>
> `method A failed → speculate about B → speculate about C → reconsider A → invent D`.
>
> When a transport/quoting/serialization layer becomes the problem, reduce complexity. Prefer writing a deterministic artifact, validating it locally, transferring it through a known-supported mechanism, then executing it, rather than nesting interpreters and escaping layers.
>
> ---

> ### 4. OPERATOR-ATTENTION BUDGET
>
> Operator attention is a scarce resource.
>
> Do **not** ask Grizz to choose routine implementation details that can be determined safely from authoritative sources or live state.
>
> Ask only when:
>
> - authority is genuinely required;
> - a consequential ambiguity cannot be resolved from evidence;
> - credentials/tokens must be director-created;
> - mutually exclusive choices have materially different consequences;
> - continuing would violate a security, identity, evidence, or rollback boundary.
>
> When operator input is required, batch known blockers whenever practical.
>
> Ask:
>
> **what fact/action is required + why execution cannot safely determine it + what remains operational meanwhile.**
>
> Do not analyze, infer, characterize, diagnose, or narrate the operator's emotional state. Treat profanity and register as communication unless the operator explicitly tells you otherwise.
>
> If ordered to cease mutation, **cease mutation immediately**. Produce only the requested handoff/receipt.

>

> `ACCEPTANCE.json`  
> `RECOVERY.json`
>
> Initialize acceptance criteria to `NOT RUN`, never optimistic defaults.
>

>

> - observed pre-state;
> - authority;
> - expected result;
> - rollback;
> - evidence location.
>

>
> OpenRig is scaffolding.

> Inspect the installed binary/version/help before assuming syntax.

>
> → `INTEGRATION`
>

That's the version I'd use.

The most important change is subtle: we're no longer merely telling the system **how the architecture should fail safely**. We're requiring the **engineering agent itself to demonstrate that it fails safely**. Your bad run is now a regression fixture. If our overnight process starts doing the equivalent of “maybe this tool works—nope—maybe heredoc—nope—maybe Bun—wait, let's reconsider…” it should detect its own thrash and fail P5 rather than burn thirty minutes of your time. fileciteturn19file2

And the good run gives us the opposite regression fixture: durable state initialized before mutation, explicit ownership, live-state revalidation, and an acceptance matrix that begins at `NOT RUN` rather than presumed success. fileciteturn19file8

**Keep the same plugin activation set:** `@gmri-engineering-operations @gmri-proxmox-control @gmri-research-evidence @gmri-spatial-systems @gmri-compute-fabric @GitHub @Remote Desktop Commander`.

Now we've actually incorporated today's field evidence instead of merely writing another prettier prompt.

For the way OMP/OpenRig is going to be used tonight, I would **not use one model everywhere**. Deliberately mixing model families gives us some protection against correlated reasoning failures—the advisor should not simply be a second copy of the primary.
