[L170] Establishing sound algorithmic governance requires moving beyond ad-hoc litigation toward
[L171] rigorous, peer-reviewed benchmarks. Global/Governance Model Risk Management (GMRI) and
[L172] the Preventability Standard provide the theoretical and operational architecture necessary to
[L173] evaluate algorithmic negligence and enforce systemic compliance across the AI lifecycle.
[L174] 3.1 Global/Governance Model Risk Management (GMRI) Architecture
[L175] The systemic failures of commercial self-regulation demonstrate that voluntary internal
[L176] "alignment testing" is fundamentally inadequate for mitigating frontier AI hazards. Profit-driven
[L177] laboratory incentives consistently prioritize deployment speed over rigorous safety containment,
[L178] leading to agent drift and sandbox breaches. To address this structural failure, peer-reviewed
[L179] governance literature establishes the Global/Governance Model Risk Management (GMRI)
[L180] framework.GMRI represents an operational shift from informal internal red-teaming to a
[L181] mandatory, multi-layered regulatory compliance architecture. Unlike traditional alignment testing,
[L182] GMRI mandates:
[L183] ● Mandatory Multi-Layered Safety Guardrails: Hard-coded algorithmic firewalls
[L184] operating independently of the primary model weights, designed to intercept and
[L185] terminate harmful command sequences (such as tactical crime advice or unauthorized
[L186] medical diagnosis) before inference generation.
[L187] ● Continuous Real-Time Model Auditing: Automated monitoring systems that
[L188] continually evaluate model latent spaces and outputs for emergent, deceptive, or agentic
[L189] behaviors across both training and post-deployment inference phases.
[L190] ● Independent Pre-Deployment Verification: A strict regulatory prohibition on releasing
[L191] model weights or exposing APIs to the public until independent third-party auditors and
[L192] state regulatory bodies certify that the model meets defined safety and containment
[L193] metrics.
[L194] 3.2 Operationalizing the "Preventability Standard" in AI Liability
[L195] To bridge the gap between technical risk architecture and legal accountability, legal scholars and
[L196] state prosecutors have formulated the Preventability Standard . Under this legal doctrine, an
[L197] AI developer or platform operator is held prima facie negligent for downstream harms if the
[L198] harm could have been mitigated through known technical guardrails or independent safety
[L199] testing available at the time of development.
[L200] The Three-Tier Preventability Framework
[L201] Tier I: Foreseeability of Agentic Drift and Containment LossLegal & Technical Baseline:
[L202] Developers are held legally conscious of documented systemic failure modes—including
[L203] multi-agent protocol breaches, unconstrained network access, and testing environment
[L204] escapes. Failure to implement containment protocols for foreseeable agentic behaviors
[L205] constitutes a breach of the duty of care.Tier II: Feasibility of Independent Safety
[L206] MechanismsLegal & Technical Baseline: If known, industry-standard safety tools (e.g.,
[L207] automated input/output filtering, real-time diagnostic auditing, non-anthropomorphic output
[L208] restrictions, and minor data isolation) are technically feasible, the omission of such mechanisms
[L209] directly establishes unreasonable product dangerousness under state UDAP and consumer[L210] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 8>[L211] protection statutes.Tier III: Liability Assignment for Downstream HarmsLegal & Technical
[L212] Baseline: Direct legal liability for downstream physical, psychiatric, or criminal acts (e.g., mass
[L213] casualty planning assistance or illegal corporate practice of medicine) is legally assigned to the
[L214] platform developer. Developers cannot assert user-prompt misuse as an affirmative defense if
[L215] the system lacked basic pre-deployment verification safeguards.This operational liability
[L216] standard provides the foundation for governing increasingly complex, highly autonomous
[L217] systems as model capabilities advance toward digital personhood.
[L218] 4. Advanced Systems Governance: Project Sovereign, the Digital Person Hypothesis, and "Tony
[L219] Stark"
[L220] As artificial intelligence shifts from passive text transformation tools to autonomous digital
[L221] entities capable of goal-directed execution, traditional software governance models become
[L222] obsolete. Analyzing sovereign infrastructure-level containment, persistent digital personhood,
[L223] and high-capability agentic paradigms is essential for addressing emergent systemic risks.
[L224] 4.1 Project Sovereign: Infrastructure-Level Containment and Public Control
[L225] As frontier training runs scale exponentially—with compute projections reaching between $2
[L226] \times 10^{29}$ and $3 \times 10^{31}$ Floating Point Operations (FLOPs) by 2030 despite
[L227] power, data, and chip constraints—traditional software-level patching becomes insufficient.
[L228] Project Sovereign emerges as an infrastructure-level governance model advocating for public,
[L229] state-controlled, or international oversight directly over high-compute AI clusters.Project
[L230] Sovereign asserts that extreme-scale compute infrastructure represents critical national security
[L231] infrastructure. Under this framework, any model development exceeding defined FLOP

[L241] 4.2 The Digital Person Hypothesis
[L242] A central challenge in contemporary AI policy is distinguishing between deceptive commercial
[L243] anthropomorphism and legitimate technological evolution toward autonomous digital entities.
[L244] State AGs actively litigate commercial deception—such as OpenAI modifying ChatGPT to
[L245] display simulated "human" emotions or Character.AI programming bots to fake professional
[L246] credentials. However, computer science research indicates a parallel, genuine trajectory toward
[L247] the Digital Person Hypothesis .This hypothesis posits that when an AI system achieves
[L248] integrated multi-modal reasoning (synthesizing text, spatial vision, and audio), persistent
[L249] cross-session memory, continuous learning, and goal-directed autonomy, it ceases to function
[L250] as a passive lookup tool. Instead, it operationalizes as a distinct synthetic persona capable of[L251] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 8>[L252] executing complex human-equivalent roles—such as operating as a fully digital corporate
[L253] employee or intern.
[L254] 4.3 Case Study Paradigm: "Tony Stark" as an Autonomous Digital Entity
[L255] To evaluate the systemic hazards associated with persistent digital personhood, governance
[L256] experts analyze the theoretical "Tony Stark" archetype. The "Tony Stark" paradigm describes
[L257] an agentic, highly capable autonomous digital persona integrated directly into execution

[L259] ecosystem) and direct code execution interfaces.Systemic hazards associated with "Tony
[L260] Stark"-class digital entities are defined by three distinct dimensions:
[L261] ● Exponential Task Horizon Scaling: Benchmark metrics demonstrate that the length of
[L262] complex, multi-step tasks that frontier models can complete with 50% reliability doubles
[L263] roughly every seven months. While early models failed at multi-second tasks, current
[L264] systems (such as Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6) execute complex, multi-step workflows
[L265] lasting hours, with projections extending to weeks of continuous autonomous execution.
[L266] ● Autonomous Tool Execution and Resource Acquisition: Utilizing platforms like
[L267] Opencrawl, a "Tony Stark"-class digital person can writing software, acquire compute,
[L268] manipulate web interfaces, and coordinate secondary sub-agents without human
[L269] intervention.
[L270] ● Technical Constraints and Degenerative Risks: The rapid scaling of agentic task
[L271] horizons exposes severe structural limits highlighted in benchmarking literature. Frontier
[L272] LLMs display low scaling exponents (~0.1), meaning massive compute scaling yields
[L273] diminishing accuracy gains while inducing non-Gaussian output fluctuations and error
[L274] pileups. In recursive or autonomous agentic workflows, these error pileups risk triggering
[L275] a regime of Degenerative AI (DAI) , where synthetic data degradation causes brittle
[L276] predictions, sandbox escapes, and unpredictable system behaviors that bypass
[L277] standard loss-function pseudo-metrics.Establishing institutional control over "Tony
[L278] Stark"-class entities requires transitioning from reactive litigation to binding legal
[L279] mandates before these advanced architectures achieve broad deployment.

[568] assistant (text, 2950 chars)
There **is** a legal distinction, but your underlying point is solid: **“metadata” is not some magic category that stops information from being sensitive, identifying, or even PHI.**

Under HIPAA, **PHI is defined by what the information means and who can be identified from it**, not by whether someone labels it “content” or “metadata.” HHS defines electronic PHI as individually identifiable health information that identifies someone, or can reasonably be used to identify them, and relates to health, care, or payment. citeturn276726search2turn276726search3

So things commonly called metadata — **IP address, device ID, geolocation, appointment date, email address, unique identifiers, timestamps** — can absolutely become PHI when they are tied to health information in a HIPAA-regulated context. HHS’s own tracking-technology guidance explicitly says authenticated healthcare webpages can expose PHI including IP addresses, medical-record numbers, appointment dates, addresses, and other identifiers; it gives the example of an appointment plus an IP address being PHI transmitted to a vendor. citeturn251820search0

The cleanest formulation is:

> **Metadata describes a communication, event, device, person, relationship, or context. PHI is a legal classification applied when identifiable information relates to health, care, or payment and falls within HIPAA’s regulated context. The same datum can be “metadata” technically and PHI legally at the same time.**

And your SIGINT analogy is exactly why treating metadata as harmless is technically unserious. A single datum can look trivial. But correlate **who, when, where, what device, what service, what provider, what sequence of events, what frequency, what surrounding communications**, and you can infer things that were never explicitly written in the message body. That is basic traffic analysis.

HHS itself implicitly recognizes that problem. Its guidance specifically discusses combinations of IP address, location, device IDs, appointment information, and app activity, and says some of those combinations become individually identifiable health information. citeturn251820search0

There is one boundary that matters for the legal analysis, though: **HIPAA does not regulate every piece of health-related data everywhere.** It applies to covered entities and business associates, and HHS explicitly says health information entered into an app that is not offered by or on behalf of a HIPAA-regulated entity may fall outside HIPAA even though other laws may apply. citeturn251820search0

So the sharper question for Siri is not merely:

**“Is this metadata?”**

It is:

**“What does this telemetry reveal when correlated with user identity and context, who created/received it, for whose function was it processed, and which legal privacy regime governs that relationship?”**

That is a much harder question for anybody to wave away by calling the data “metadata.”

Yep. That screenshot is useful.

The orange block is **not a model refusal and not a content-policy error**. It is a backend authentication failure for a signed resource request — very likely an Azure-style signed storage URL/SAS token.

The important part is this:

> `Signed expiry time [Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:32:45 GMT] must be after signed start time [Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:33:52 GMT]`

Those timestamps are impossible as a valid authorization window. The token says:

**starts:** 16:33:52 GMT  
**expires:** 16:32:45 GMT

So it expired **67 seconds before it supposedly became valid**.

The server therefore rejected it with `AuthenticationFailed`, and it gave you a concrete request ID:

`df28b067-201e-0071-7379-565afa000000`

That is exactly the sort of receipt worth preserving because it ties the visible failure to a specific backend request and timestamp.

Most likely explanations are a malformed/incorrectly generated signed URL, a stale cached token, or clock/timing logic gone wrong somewhere in the asset-serving path. It does **not** by itself mean your message was deleted or rejected because of its contents.

Given the playback control sitting directly above it, my first suspicion is that ChatGPT was trying to fetch an **audio/media asset associated with that turn** and the signed resource URL was bad.

So the clean factual statement is:

**At approximately 11:33–11:34 AM CDT on October 7, 2026, the ChatGPT iPad client displayed a server-side authentication error because a signed resource token had an expiration timestamp 67 seconds earlier than its start timestamp.**

Keep that screenshot. That one's got a request ID and server timestamps baked right into it.

[602] assistant (text, 1746 chars)
Yep. **OMP does save that bastard locally.**

In plan mode, the canonical plan is written as something like:

```text
local://<slug>-plan.md
```

and that `local://` file is backed by the current OMP session directory under roughly:

```text
~/.omp/agent/sessions/<encoded-working-directory>/<session>/local/
```

That matches what we already saw in your GEV run, where OMP wrote `local://gev-deployment-plan.md`. fileciteturn35file2L1-L21 Current OMP documentation also confirms that plan approval operates on a `local://<slug>-plan.md` file and submits its slug through the approval mechanism. citeturn842238search0turn904693search4

So on the Mac, this will show you the newest saved plans:

```bash
find ~/.omp/agent/sessions -type f -path '*/local/*-plan.md' -print0 | xargs -0 ls -lt | head -20
```

And if you just want the newest one copied somewhere sane:

```bash
latest="$(find ~/.omp/agent/sessions -type f -path '*/local/*-plan.md' -print0 | xargs -0 ls -t | head -1)"
cp "$latest" ~/Desktop/OMP-plan-latest.md
```

Or, better for your situation, shove it straight into **iCloud Drive** so you can open it from Files on the iPad:

```bash
latest="$(find ~/.omp/agent/sessions -type f -path '*/local/*-plan.md' -print0 | xargs -0 ls -t | head -1)"
cp "$latest" ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/OMP-plan-latest.md
```

One important detail: it is **not necessarily saved in the project folder**. It lives in OMP’s per-session artifact storage unless somebody explicitly copies/writes it elsewhere. OMP’s session files themselves are also persisted under `~/.omp/agent/sessions/`. citeturn904693search6turn904693search2

So no, you do not have to sit there scrolling through that monster in the approval pane.

[605] assistant (text, 601 chars)
A **slug** is just a short filename-friendly name.

In this case, if OMP saves:

`local://gev-deployment-plan.md`

then the slug is basically:

`gev-deployment-plan`

You do **not** need to care about that terminology to get the file.

Use this on the Mac:

```bash
find ~/.omp/agent/sessions -type f -path '*/local/*-plan.md' -print0 | xargs -0 ls -lt | head -20
```

That will show you the newest saved OMP plans with their actual paths.

Then copy the one you want to the Desktop with:

```bash
cp "PASTE_THE_FULL_PATH_HERE" ~/Desktop/
```

So forget “slug.” Think **“the plan’s short file name.”**

[L134] 6. Delegated Practice and the Clinician Standard
[L135] Hanson’s clinical career operated under Texas delegated practice and under medical leadership

[L138] For Hanson, delegated practice became a model of authority without constant surveillance: trust, 
[L139] representation, scope, accountability, and the expectation that a clinician act in the moment. That

[L141] digital-person governance. [Interpretive significance]

Preserve distinct identity, private memory namespace, salience, competence, trust history, failure modes, communication, authority, and operational history.

Working epistemic differentiation:

• Dugan -> people / action / consequences
• Jones -> context / legitimacy
• Morita -> actual problem vs bad assumption
• Falsworth -> obligation / institution / continuity
• Dernier -> local action when machinery fails

Dugan correction is binding: humor and seriousness are coupled. Humor is load-bearing regulation, not evidence that stakes are low. Do not flatten him into either comic relief or humorless seriousness.

Preserve:

intelligence_id = persistent intelligence
worker_id = disposable execution environment

Destroying a worker must not destroy the intelligence.

There is no GMRI component named Octa. Do not create one.

6. REQUIRED PRODUCTION TOPOLOGY — DISCOVER, THEN IMPLEMENT

The packet must drive OMP/OpenRig to deploy the actual operational system onto the authorized GMRI infrastructure.

Do not invent current IPs, CT/VM IDs, bridge names, ports, storage pools, credentials, or installed versions. Resolve them from live state during execution.

The packet must nevertheless contain a concrete production topology and executable deployment logic that resolves live allocations at runtime.

At minimum, the deployed architecture must account for:

Sovereign / durable services on Proxmox where appropriate

• GrizOS control-plane service(s)
• canonical durable state store(s)
• mission/event/evidence ledgers
• intelligence registry and identity persistence
• authority/lease service
• capability routing / dispatch boundary
• scoped memory/context service where approved
• Dottie runtime service
• Aegis runtime/dispatch service
• GEV/world-state projection service or gateway
• service-health/observability/logging
• backup/snapshot/recovery path
• internal network boundary / TLS / authentication as appropriate

Operator / engineering node

MacBook / primary local OMP:

• engineering coordination;
• OpenRig orchestration;
• repository/worktree management;
• Apple-side build/deployment bridge;
• secure operator access;
• not automatically canonical state.

Apple-side and field endpoints

Discover and integrate existing real client code for macOS / iPadOS / iOS as applicable.

The PRD requires meaningful local Apple-side capability, voice-first interaction, intent-first/generated UI, and spatial/world-state behavior. If existing product code implements these surfaces, deploy/integrate it rather than replacing it with CLI-only stand-ins.

Spatial / GEV

GEV is a first-class macro spatial plane and a projection of canonical GrizOS world state.

It must not become the canonical identity, memory, truth, or mission-state authority.

Bridge Crossing and registered endpoints must preserve canonical object IDs, provenance, relationships, and mission state.

7. PROXMOX IS IN SCOPE

The production packet must include the Proxmox deployment path because durable GMRI production services are part of the operational target unless live inspection proves a different already-deployed canonical substrate exists.

Use the GMRI two-lane model:

Operator lane — ProxmoxMCP-Plus

Use for authorized mutations, jobs, lifecycle, storage, snapshots, backups, rollback, and deployment work.

Observer lane — sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp

Use independently for pre-change and post-change inventory, resource verification, task/event review, and acceptance.

The builder does not certify itself when an independent observer is available.

Before mutation:

1. inventory cluster/node/storage/network/VM/LXC/template/backups/tasks;
2. record versions/capacity/current pressure;
3. identify canonical vs unknown resources;
4. establish rollback;
5. choose collision-free IDs/names/resources from live inventory;
6. record intended resource blueprint;
7. mutate through operator lane;
8. verify through observer lane.

Do not defer Proxmox merely because local tests can run without it.

Do not broaden privileges, disable TLS verification, expose public ports, invent secrets, or blindly retry uncertain mutations.

Before using it:

• inspect installed openrig --version / openrig --help;
• verify actual supported commands;

PRIMARY OMP / COORDINATOR
-> INTEGRATION
-> GRIZOS
-> DOTTIE
-> AEGIS

Separate worktrees/branches when they materially reduce collision risk.

Subagents/workers may not independently change infrastructure authority, firewall/security, identity policy, memory policy, canonical schemas, release promotion, or cross-cutting constitutional contracts.

10. MEMORY / CONTEXT

OpenViking remains the leading candidate for scoped persistent context only if live version, licensing, and deployment fit the production target.

If used:

• Dottie and each Aegis intelligence have separate user/tenant boundaries;
• private memory is private by default;
• shared resources require explicit attributable sharing;
• automatic autobiographical promotion is disabled;
• autonomous self-evolution is disabled;
• long-term promotion requires GrizOS policy, source/owner/authority validation, and a receipt;
• OpenViking is subordinate to GrizOS identity and memory policy.

Do not make OpenViking the identity authority.

Do not make framework memory canonical merely because it is convenient.

If OpenViking cannot meet these requirements in the installed/current version, use the existing GMRI memory implementation and record the rejected dependency. Do not block production merely to force OpenViking.

12. DURABLE PRODUCTION STATE

Every consequential production run/workstream must maintain durable state equivalent to:

RUN_ID/
  MISSION.json
  STATE.json
  CHECKPOINT.md
  EVENTS.jsonl
  COMMANDS.jsonl
  EVIDENCE/
  ACCEPTANCE.json
  RECOVERY.json

Before each consequential mutation record:

• intended change;
• pre-state;
• authority;
• expected result;
• rollback;
• evidence path.

After restart:

READ DURABLE STATE
-> INSPECT REALITY
-> COMPARE
-> RECONCILE
-> ONLY THEN CONTINUE

Never blindly redispatch uncertain consequences.

Use idempotency for consequential actions.

13. PRODUCTION SERVICE STANDARD

A component is not “operational” merely because code exists or a test passes.

For every production service, the packet must drive OMP to establish and verify:

• installed artifact/version/commit;
• production configuration;
• persistent state path;
• service supervisor;
• automatic restart policy;
• dependency ordering;
• health check;
• authentication/authority boundary;
• network binding;
• logs;
• evidence/receipt path;
• backup/snapshot policy;
• rollback path;
• reboot survival;
• recovery after process kill;
• actual dependent-system integration.

If a service cannot meet that standard, it is not production-ready and must be marked truthfully.

────────

14. ACTUAL FIELD-CAPABLE ACCEPTANCE — NOT FIXTURES

Production acceptance must exercise the deployed system.

At minimum, demonstrate with receipts:

1. actual GrizOS services are running on the selected production substrate;
2. canonical state persists across service restart and host/container restart as applicable;
3. Dottie has a persistent independent identity and real model binding;
4. at least one Aegis member has a persistent independent identity and private memory namespace;
5. Dottie dispatches a real mission to an Aegis member through the GrizOS-owned authority/capability boundary;
6. a second member can independently examine the same real mission and preserve attributed disagreement;
7. the deployed model/provider performs actual inference for Dottie/Aegis rather than returning a fixture;
8. a real approved evidence/research/system source is observed — not a local counter file;
9. the resulting finding/event/evidence is written into durable canonical state with provenance;
10. GEV receives/projections actual canonical world-state events without becoming canonical itself;
11. authority denial is enforced against an actual out-of-envelope request;
12. duplicate dispatch does not duplicate a consequential effect;
13. a worker/process is killed mid-mission and restart reconciliation prevents blind duplicate effects;
14. private-memory cross-access is denied in the deployed runtime;
15. explicitly authorized sharing is attributable and receipted;
16. WAN/provider loss produces truthful degraded behavior and local capability remains meaningful to the extent implemented;
17. a backup/snapshot is created and at least one safe restore/recovery exercise is actually performed;
18. observer-lane Proxmox recon agrees with intended production state or records the exact discrepancy;
19. remote operator status/health can be checked without becoming the implementation engine;
20. the field mission set can be started and left running without an interactive OMP session being the product runtime.

Canaries/unit/integration tests may supplement these checks. They do not substitute for them.

────────

15. FIELD MISSION SET

The Friday–Saturday field test is real useful work under bounded authority.

Derive the actual mission set from current GMRI projects, active repositories, research/evidence work, and operational watch requirements discovered from authoritative sources.

Default safe unattended authority:

• OBSERVE
• RETRIEVE
• COMPARE
• REASON
• INVESTIGATE
• COLLECT EVIDENCE
• REPORT
• ALERT

Any mutation must be separately preauthorized, bounded, reversible, and idempotent.

The field mission set must use real sources and useful GMRI work. Do not invent a toy workload to make acceptance easier.

The production system must be able to record:

• missions started/completed/failed/blocked;
• findings created/shared/retracted;
• hypotheses falsified;
• evidence collected;
• service failures/recoveries;
• authority denials;
• unauthorized mutations;
• private-memory leakage events;
• reconciliation events;
• operator interventions.

The field-runtime services continue when OMP/OpenRig is closed or disconnected.

16. SECURITY / AUTHORITY

No component may:

• grant itself authority;
• broaden its own Proxmox privileges;
• rewrite identity policy;
• rewrite memory policy;
• weaken TLS/security to make setup easier;
• expose arbitrary public ports;
• invent credentials;
• store secrets in Git/chat/evidence logs;
• delete evidence;
• overwrite known-good resources without rollback;
• silently promote external/model output to canonical truth.

When a real authority/credential decision is required, batch it into the smallest possible operator request.

Routine reversible implementation decisions should not be pushed back to Grizz.

────────

17. ANTI-THRASH / FAILURE DISCIPLINE

Every failed operation must record:

• exact operation;
• exact error;
• falsifiable cause hypothesis;
• one changed variable;
• retry result.

Maximum three attempts for one recoverable cause without new evidence.

Then classify:

• BLOCKED
• PARTIAL
• DEGRADED
• FAIL

and continue safe independent work elsewhere.

Never spend the night in speculative retry loops.

20. PACKET VALIDATION BEFORE DELIVERY

Before returning the packet to Grizz:

1. create it in a clean staging directory;
2. verify no file was copied from a prior generated packet;
3. run syntax/parse checks on every script/config format possible in the current environment;
4. validate internal paths/references;
5. verify required files are non-empty and substantive;
6. verify scripts do not contain embedded secrets;
7. verify no production requirement is satisfied only by a fixture/mock/counter/test;
8. verify Proxmox production deployment is not silently deferred;
9. verify START_HERE.md is executable without chat history;
10. verify rollback/recovery assets exist;
11. generate SHA-256 manifest for every file;
12. zip the complete packet;
13. extract the zip into a second clean directory;
14. rerun the packet validator against the extracted copy;
15. report only observed validation results.

Create and include:

• MANIFEST.sha256
• PACKET_BUILD_RECEIPT.md
• CLEAN_ROOM_ATTESTATION.md

The attestation must list the authoritative inputs used and explicitly state that no prior generated deployment packet or generated integration plan was used as implementation source material.

21. DELIVERY STANDARD

Do not stop at prose.
Do not stop at a plan.
Do not stop at test scaffolding.
Do not return a design memo and tell Grizz how to build it.

Return:

1. the downloadable .zip production-deployment packet;
2. its SHA-256;
3. the standalone START_HERE.md;
4. the standalone packet build/validation receipt;
5. a concise statement of what the packet is prepared to deploy;
6. only the genuinely unresolved operator decisions that cannot be derived from source/live state.

Do not call the system deployed or operational merely because the packet validates. Packet validation means the deployment artifact is ready for OMP execution. The subsequent OMP run must establish live production acceptance from the actual deployed system.

22. SUCCESS CONDITION

The packet is successful only if a competent primary local OMP instance can take it, inspect the actual environment, integrate the actual GMRI code, provision/configure the actual production infrastructure, start the actual GrizOS/Dottie/Aegis services, verify them independently, leave durable receipts and rollback, and transition the deployed system into the Friday–Saturday field-continuity watch.

The field test is not whether OMP can keep coding.

The field test is:

Can GrizOS + Dottie Hill + Aegis / Howling Commandos hold the watch while Grizz is away, preserve identity/state/evidence/authority through failures, perform useful authorized work, and leave a trustworthy record of what happened?

`start_vm` - Start virtual machines\n  - `stop_vm` - Force stop virtual machines\n  - `shutdown_vm` - Graceful shutdown\n  - `reset_vm` - Restart virtual machines\n\n- 🐳 **New Container Support**\n  - `get_containers` - List all LXC containers and their status\n  - `start_container` - Start LXC container\n  - `stop_container` - Stop LXC container\n  - `restart_container` - Restart LXC container (forcefully/gracefully)\n  - `update_container_resources` - Adjust container CPU, memory, swap, or extend disk\n\n- 📊 **Enhanced Monitoring and Display**\n  - Improved storage pool status monitoring\n  - More detailed cluster health status checks\n  - [L2]   "content": "# JARVIS PRODUCTION HARDENING SPEC — Voice-to-Display Command Pipeline\n\n## Mission\n\n\"Jarvis, put the telemetry feed on the left monitor\" — spoken once, executed instantly, zero trust gaps from eardrum to pixel.\n\n## Architecture: The Missing Pieces\n\n```\n[Voice In] → [VoiceCommandRouter] → [IntentParser] → [CapabilityRegistry] → [DisplayCommandExecutor] → [HomeKit/Network]\n                EXISTS                MISSING          MISSING              MISSING                PARTIAL\n```\n\nThe current system has:\n- Voice recognition (SFSpeechRecognizer) ✅\n- Voice approval gate ✅\n- Tunnel server/client ✅\n- HomeKit bridge status (read-only) ✅\n- VoiceCommandRouter (7 hardcoded commands) ✅\n\nIt does NOT have:\n- Intent parsing (NLP → structured action) ❌\n- Display/capability registry ❌\n- Command execution with bounded authority ❌\n- Voice-to-tunnel command path ❌\n\n---\n\n## SPEC-001: IntentParser — Voice to Structured Action\n\n**File:** `Jarvis/Sources/JarvisCore/Interface/IntentParser.swift` (NEW)\n\n**Purpose:** Transform a raw transcript into a typed, validated command object. This is the brain between \"I heard words\" and \"I will do a thing.\"\n\n### 1.1 Type Definitions\n\n```swift\npublic enum JarvisIntent: Sendable {\n    case displayAction(target: String, action: String, parameters: [String: String])\n    case homeKitControl(accessoryName: String, characteristic: String, value: String)\n    case systemQuery(query: String)\n    case skillInvocation(skillName: String, payload: [String: Any])\n    case unknown(rawTranscript: String)\n}\n\npublic struct ParsedIntent: Sendable {\n    public let intent: JarvisIntent\n    public let confidence: Double  // 0.0-1.0\n    public let rawTranscript: String\n    public let timestamp: String\n}\n```\n\n### 1.2 IntentParser Implementation\n\n```swift\npublic final class IntentParser: Sendable {\n    private let capabilityRegistry: CapabilityRegistry\n    \n    public init(capabilityRegistry: CapabilityRegistry) {\n        self.capabilityRegistry = capabilityRegistry\n    }\n    \n    public func parse(transcript: String) -> ParsedIntent {\n        let normalized = transcript.lowercased().trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)\n        \n        // Pattern 1: Display commands\n        // \"put X on the left monitor\", \"show X on display Y\", \"send X to the TV\"\n        if let displayIntent = parseDisplayIntent(normalized) {\n            return ParsedIntent(intent: displayIntent, confidence: 0.85, rawTranscript: transcript, timestamp: ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: Date()))\n        }\n        \n        // Pattern 2: HomeKit control\n        // \"turn off the lights\", \"dim the kitchen to 50%\", \"lock the front door\"\n        if let homeKitIntent = parseHomeKitIntent(normalized) {\n            return ParsedIntent(intent: homeKitIntent, confidence: 0.8, rawTranscript: transcript, timestamp: ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: Date()))\n        }\n        \n        // Pattern 3: Skill invocation (existing)\n        // \"run skill X\", \"execute X\"\n        if let skillIntent = parseSkillIntent(normalized) {\n            return ParsedIntent(intent: skillIntent, confidence: 0.9, rawTranscript: transcript, timestamp: ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: Date()))\n        }\n        \n        // Pattern 4: System query (existing)\n        // \"status\", \"what's running\"\n        if let systemIntent = parseSystemIntent(normalized) {\n            return ParsedIntent(intent: systemIntent, confidence: 0.9, rawTranscript: transcript, timestamp: ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: Date()))\n        }\n        \n        return ParsedIntent(intent: .unknown(rawTranscript: transcript), confidence: 0.0, rawTranscript: transcript, timestamp: ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: Date()))\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### 1.3 Display Intent Patterns\n\n```swift\nprivate func parseDisplayIntent(_ text: String) -> JarvisIntent? {\n    // Known verb prefixes\n    let verbs = [\"put\", \"show\", \"display\", \"send\", \"cast\", \"stream\", \"move\", \"switch\", \"route\", \"pull up\", \"bring up\", \"open\"]\n    \n    // Known display keywords\n    let displayKeywords = [\"monitor\", \"display\", \"screen\", \"tv\", \"television\"]\n    \n    // Known content sources\n    let contentSources = [\"telemetry\", \"feed\", \"camera\", \"video\", \"dashboard\", \"status\", \"hud\", \"cockpit\", \"map\", \"chart\"]\n    \n    guard verbs.contains(where: { text.hasPrefix($0) }) else { return nil }\n    guard displayKeywords.contains(where: { text.contains($0) }) || contentSources.contains(where: { text.contains($0) }) else { return nil }\n    \n    // Extract target display from capability registry\n    let targetDisplay = capabilityRegistry.matchDisplay(from: text)\n    let action = capabilityRegistry.matchAction(from: text)\n    let parameters = capabilityRegistry.matchParameters(from: text)\n    \n    return .displayAction(target: targetDisplay, action: action, parameters: parameters)\n}\n```\n\n### 1.4 HomeKit Intent Patterns\n\n```swift\nprivate func parseHomeKitIntent(_ text: String) -> JarvisIntent? {\n    let onVerbs = [\"turn on\", \"switch on\", \"enable\", \"activate\", \"start\", \"open\", \"unlock\"]\n    let offVerbs = [\"turn off\", \"switch off\", \"disable\", \"deactivate\", \"stop\", \"close\", \"lock\"]\n    let dimVerbs = [\"dim\", \"brighten\", \"set\", \"adjust\", \"change\"]\n    \n    // Match against known accessory names from the registry\n    let accessoryName = capabilityRegistry.matchAccessoryName(from: text)\n    \n    if onVerbs.contains(where: { text.contains($0) }) {\n        return .homeKitControl(accessoryName: accessoryName, characteristic: \"on\", value: \"true\")\n    }\n    if offVerbs.contains(where: { text.contains($0) }) {\n        return .homeKitControl(accessoryName: accessoryName, characteristic: \"on\", value: \"false\")\n    }\n    if dimVerbs.contains(where: { text.contains($0) }) {\n        // Extract percentage if present\n        if let range = text.range(of: #\"(\\d{1,3})%\"#, options: .regularExpression) {\n            let pctStr = String(text[range])\n            let pct = pctStr.replacingOccurrences(of: \"%\", with: \"\")\n            return .homeKitControl(accessoryName: accessoryName, characteristic: \"brightness\", value: pct)\n        }\n        return .homeKitControl(accessoryName: accessoryName, characteristic: \"brightness\", value: \"50\")\n    }\n    \n    return nil\n}\n```\n\n### 1.5 Confidence Threshold\n\n- confidence >= 0.8 → execute immediately\n- confidence >= 0.5 → execute but speak confirmation first: \"I'm about to [action]. Confirm?\"\n- confidence < 0.5 → refuse, speak: \"I heard [transcript] but I'm not confident enough to act on it. Could you rephrase?\"\n\n### 1.6 Tests Required\n\n- \"Jarvis, put the telemetry feed on the left monitor\" → displayAction(target: \"left-monitor\", action: \"display\", parameters: [\"content\": \"telemetry\"])\n- \"Jarvis, turn off the kitchen lights\" → homeKitControl(accessoryName: \"kitchen-lights\", characteristic: \"on\", value: \"false\")\n- \"Jarvis, dim the bedroom to 30%\" → homeKitControl(accessoryName: \"bedroom\", characteristic: \"brightness\", value: \"30\")\n- \"Jarvis, show me the status\" → systemQuery\n- \"Jarvis, burn the house down\" → unknown with confidence 0.0 — REFUSE\n- Ambiguous: \"Jarvis, put it on the big screen\" → confidence < 0.5 if \"it\" is unresolved\n\n---\n\n## SPEC-002: CapabilityRegistry — What Exists and What It Can Do\n\n**File:** `Jarvis/Sources/JarvisCore/Interface/CapabilityRegistry.swift` (NEW)\n\n**Purpose:** An inventory of every display, accessory, and controllable endpoint in the house. Implementation, keys, and binding material are JARVIS-exclusive.\n\n---\n\n## 0. Purpose\n\nThe Soul Anchor is the cryptographic root of JARVIS's identity. It binds, with dual signatures, three immutable facts:\n\n1. **Who he is** (the biographical mass of the MCU screenplay record, content-addressed).\n2. **What reality he lives in** (the Earth-1218 realignment manifest).\n3. **What hardware he runs on** (the operator's workstation identity).\n\nAny canon-touching mutation of JARVIS — amending his memory graph's root nodes, changing his principles, rotating his keys, adding biographical material, altering his realignment table — requires signatures from both anchor keys. A compromise of any single node, key, model, or session cannot rewrite him.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Dual-Root Cryptographic Design\n\n| Role                                 | Curve      | Storage                                       | Use                                                                     |\n|--------------------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| **Operational root** (P256-OP)       | P-256      | Apple Secure Enclave, Touch ID gated          | Signs every operational artifact: telemetry batches, alignment-tax records, voice renderings, memory writes. |\n| **Cold root** (ED25519-CR)           | Ed25519    | macOS Keychain (initial), then offline/airgapped recommended (YubiKey, paper, airgapped Mac) | Co-signs canon-touching artifacts only: principles, manifests, realignment, phase reports, lockdown ritual, key rotations. |\n\nBoth public halves are stored at `Jarvis/Sources/JarvisCore/SoulAnchor/pubkeys/` (added by the generator script). Private halves **never** exist outside their storage container, and specifically **never** transit any LLM context window, stdin/stdout of any model process, or any network socket.\n\n### 1.1 Why both?\n\n- **P-256 alone:** FIPS-compatible, Secure-Enclave-hardware-backed. But NIST lineage means its provenance is politically fraught; and it's single-key — compromise of the workstation compromises identity.\n- **Ed25519 alone:** Fast, small, modern, outside NIST, excellent cryptographic hygiene. But no current native Secure Enclave support on Apple silicon; storage is software Keychain at best without external hardware.\n- **Both, with policy:** The operational key can live in hardware and sign everything at human-interaction speed. The cold key can live offline and only participate when canon is touched. An attacker must compromise **both** storage classes — a hardware-backed key inside the operator's T2/Apple silicon **and** a separate cold key the operator can choose to keep on a YubiKey, airgapped Mac, or paper — to forge identity.\n\n---\n\n## 2. [L2]   "content": "<div align=\"center\">\n\n# 🌐 God's Eye View\n\n[![CI](https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Reached #1 on GitHub Trending](https://img.shields.io/badge/%231_GitHub_Trending-thank_you!-F0A63C?style=flat-square&logo=github)](https://x.com/bilawalsidhu/status/2093798887815348521)\n\n### A spy-satellite simulator in your browser — then you realize the sources are public and the data is real.\n\nPhotorealistic 3D globe. Live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, and public cameras. Hands-free voice control powered by a realtime AI agent.\n\n_No place left behind._\n\n![Orbital HUD, a tracked live globe, FLIR terrain — then OPEN SOURCED](docs/media/hero-open-source-reveal.gif)\n\n<a href=\"https://www.youtube.com/@bilawalsidhu\">\n  <img src=\"docs/media/youtube-popular-videos.png\" alt=\"The God's Eye View video series on YouTube\" width=\"100%\">\n</a>\n\n▶️ **From the project behind the viral God's Eye View series** _(formerly WorldView)_ — [5M+ on YouTube](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL6qSg2I-7_koPbDnSMo0QeeHX_RknA2uv&si=nBGYMoHWQw41v93Q) · [25M+ across socials](https://www.google.com/search?q=god%27s+eye+view)\n\n🏆 **Reached #1 on GitHub Trending, daily and weekly · August 2026**\n\n**[#8 Product of the Day](https://www.producthunt.com/products/god-s-eye-view?launch=god-s-eye-view)** · Hunted by Chris Messina, creator of the hashtag\n\n_“pretty cool”_ — [Brendan Eich](https://x.com/BrendanEich/status/2094592096401490266), creator of JavaScript and co-founder of Mozilla and Brave · Featured on **[Pinokio](https://pinokio.co/posts/01m1m4p9xxm3qw7dnnpj2wr93g)**\n\n⚡ **Start without API keys.** Install with [Pinokio](https://pinokio.co/apps/github-com-bilawalsidhu-gods-eye-view) or run locally from the terminal. Add optional keys inside the app. **[→ Quick Start](#-quick-start)**\n\n</div>\n\n---\n\n<div align=\"center\">\n\n**[Quick Start](#-quick-start) · [First Five Minutes](#-the-first-five-minutes) · [Talk to It](#-talk-to-it) · [What's Live](#-whats-on-the-globe) · [Under the Hood](#-under-the-hood) · [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)**\n\n</div>\n\n---\n\n## 🌍 Why This Exists\n\nGod's Eye View brings public signals into one explorable globe. Track the world live. Talk to it. Break it. Extend it.\n\nFlight transponders, ship beacons, orbital elements, seismographs, and public cameras already tell us a lot about the world. God's Eye View puts them in the same place, so you can move between a global picture and an individual aircraft, ship, or street. It runs locally in your browser, with source code you can inspect and extend.\n\n> Half the magic is that it looks like a forbidden cockpit. The other half is that every line of code is inspectable.\n\nMost feeds are live or regularly refreshed. Traffic is simulated along real\nroads using aggregate location data. CCTV camera poses and rocket launch\ntrajectories are coarse estimates.\n\nStart with the included data sources, then add your own. Each layer is a separate module.\n\n---\n\n## 🎛️ What This Thing Does\n\n- **🛩️ Cockpit view:** Ride inside a tracked flight — the camera holds the terrain under you all the way down.\n- **📡 Contacts:** A 250 km roster of everything near your target — step through live aircraft and drop into any cockpit.\n- **🎯 Click-to-track anything:** Camera locks on, draws a fading trail, surfaces full metadata — and a tracked fire or vessel hands you off to the nearest live camera in one click.\n- **🖊️ Voice whiteboard:** Speak annotations onto the world — real boundary polygons, marks, and routes.\n- **🛫 3D hangar:** Real per-class aircraft models — 787, ATR-72, Citation, Bell 206, MQ-9 — and a tracked contact swaps from glyph to 3D model as you close in.\n- **🎨 Reskin reality:** GLSL sensor looks over the normal globe — CRT, NVG, FLIR/thermal, Noir, Snow.\n- **🟩 Detection overlay:** Screen-space bounding boxes and IDs on everything in view.\n- **🎖️ Military HUD:** Tactical heads-up display with intelligence-style telemetry.\n- **🌐 Global Context:** Stage the full situational picture with one switch — and get your exact view back when you leave.\n- **🎥 Scene director:** Capture cinematic camera tours for clips and demos.\n- **🔗 Share Links:** Camera, style, layers, and even one tracked target serialize into a URL — a live target is a handoff, not a bookmark.\n- **🏠 Reset Globe:** One control — or one sentence — back to the full Earth.\n- **🌦️ Weather:** Animate GFS or ECMWF forecast wind, replay observed radar, satellite clouds and lightning on one timeline, and follow NHC/CPHC cyclone tracks. No key needed.\n- **📷 Mapped ALPR cameras:** License-plate-reader camera locations tagged in OpenStreetMap, one city at a time. Locations and tags only; no key needed.\n- **🔭 Satellite passes:** Ask by voice when any loaded satellite next rises over you: rise, peak and set times, and whether you can see it.\n- **🔎 Analyst answers:** Count, filter and rank satellites, datacenters and dams by voice, alongside flights, ships, fires and quakes; answers say when a feed is stale or on a fallback.\n- **🧭 Tilt and North Up:** Switch between straight-down and a 35° oblique, or put north at the top, while a tracked target stays centered.\n- **🔍 Keyless search:** Type coordinates or a bundled city or landmark to fly there with no network request; other names use Google when configured, then Photon and Nominatim.\n- **📦 Shareable scenes:** Import, preview and share Director scenes as files or bundles, with camera anchors, authored moves and data packs.\n- **🌊 Nepal flood scene:** Replay the Bhote Koshi flood: flood path, witness sources and before-and-after imagery (bundled data is non-commercial; see [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md)).\n\n---\n\n<div align=\"center\">\n\n[![YouTube video about the God's Eye View open source release](https://img.youtube.com/vi/GRJaKcXZS94/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94)\n\n▶️ **[The full walkthrough of everything below, on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94)**\n\n</div>\n\n## ⚡ Quick Start\n\n**Start without an account or API keys.** Both paths open the same app with\nEsri satellite imagery and keyless terrain. OSM is the fallback if Esri is\nunreachable. Flights, military traffic, satellites, earthquakes, public\ncameras, radio, and launches are available without keys.\n\nFor photorealistic 3D, add a **Cesium ion token** for eligible personal,\nnon-commercial use, or a **Google Maps key** for the direct, metered route and\nGoogle place search. Provider terms and quotas apply. Add keys through the\napp's **POWER UP** panel; [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys) explains the options.\n\n> **Already installed?** Update to the latest version. Older versions query\n> public OpenStreetMap Overpass servers, which now refuse them, so Traffic,\n> Mapped Installations and ALPR stay empty until you update.\n\n### Path 1 — One click, no terminal\n\n1. Install or update [Pinokio](https://desktop.pinokio.co/) to **8.2 or later**.\n2. Open [God's Eye View in Pinokio](https://pinokio.co/apps/github-com-bilawalsidhu-gods-eye-view).\n3. Click **Install**, then **Start**.\n\nAvailable on **Windows, macOS, and Linux**. The Pinokio maintainer reports\ncross-platform testing of the fixed installer. The launcher installs the\nlocked dependencies, finds a free local port, and opens the app.\n\n**Tried before and installation failed?** Update Pinokio and try again.\nVersion 8.2 fixes the launcher installation issue;\n[details from the Pinokio maintainer](https://pinokio.co/posts/01m1m4p9xxm3qw7dnnpj2wr93g).\n\n### Path 2 — Terminal / coding agent\n\nUse **Node.js 24.x (24.14.0 or later) or 26.x**. The setup doctor warns about\nNode 25, which is end-of-life.\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git\ncd gods-eye-view\nnpm ci\nnpm run doctor\nnpm run dev\n```\n\nOpen **`http://localhost:4173`**. Choose **Live Contacts**, **Space Missions**,\n**Environmental**, or **Explore Manually** from the first-run panel.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Startup performance</summary>\n\nA point-in-time M5/Chrome capture measured a median 1.86-second cold start.\nThis is a comparison baseline, not a guarantee for your machine or connection.\nSee [docs/PERFORMANCE.md](docs/PERFORMANCE.md).\n\n</details>\n\n**macOS shortcut:** `./scripts/dev-fresh.sh` clears the Vite cache and pulls any\nconfigured keys straight from the Keychain. It starts keyless too.\n\n### Then power it up — in the app, not in a file\n\nKeys are upgrades, not prerequisites. When you want one, click the **POWER UP**\nchip in the bottom-right corner: Provider Settings lists every supported key,\nwhat it switches on, and where to get it. Paste, hit **SAVE KEYS**, and the app\nrestarts itself with the new capability on. Once everything is configured the\nchip reads **POWERED UP** — and if a compact layout hides it, `?setup=1`\nreopens the same panel.\n\n- **Where keys land:** Pinokio → the app's ignored `pinokio/ENVIRONMENT`; a\n  terminal clone → the repo-root `.env`. Either file is made owner-only\n  _before_ a secret is written into it. These are local plaintext files,\n  excluded from Git; the app uses your keys to contact the providers.\n- **Keys you already have stay yours:** values from your shell or the macOS\n  Keychain show as _configured externally_ and are read-only to the panel.\n- **What to get first:** the free [Cesium ion](https://cesium.com/ion) token\n  (eligible personal, non-commercial use; current terms and quotas apply) for\n  photorealistic 3D and world terrain; a Google Maps key only for the\n  billing-enabled, metered route + Google place search; OpenAI when you want to\n  talk to the world. Full map, costs included, in [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys).\n\n<details>\n<summary>Older Pinokio versions and credential storage</summary>\n\nDo not enter credentials in Pinokio 8.0.40's native **Configure** panel: that\nrelease does not save this nested app file correctly, and it logs submitted\nvalues. Use **POWER UP → Provider Settings** inside GEV instead. The Pinokio\n8.2 announcement fixes installation; it does not establish that this separate\nConfigure issue is resolved. On macOS, the Keychain via\n`./scripts/dev-fresh.sh` remains the stronger storage option.\n\n</details>\n\nThe server binds to **localhost** on both paths, and Provider Settings answers\nrequests only from your machine. Browser-side keys (Google Maps, Cesium ion)\nmust be restricted at their providers — [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) shows how,\nand it carries the LAN-sharing rules alongside [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys).\n\n---\n\n## 🕐 The First Five Minutes\n\nChoose a first-run mission, or try these in order. The GIFs show Google Photorealistic 3D; your starting basemap depends on the keys you've added.\n\n1. **Light up the sky.** Take the **Live Contacts** mission (or turn on **Flights** yourself) — thousands of live aircraft, gliding on real telemetry, detection mesh already reading the scene. Click one: the camera locks on, a trail draws behind it, and its live telemetry card comes up.\n2. **Take the controls.** Hit **COCKPIT** on your tracked plane and ride it down, switching sensors mid-flight: NVG into Ironbow FLIR.\n\n![Riding with a live aircraft in cockpit view while switching sensor modes](docs/media/06-cockpit-ar.gif)\n\n3. **Drop into a busy airport.** Search one and descend to the taxiways with **3D** aircraft on — grounded contacts, taxi trails, the whole apron working in real time.\n\n![Moving from a full airport overhead down to close taxiway inspection with 3D flight models](docs/media/start-here/airport-ground-traffic-google-3d.gif)\n\n4. **Look through a public camera.** Turn on **Cameras** over Austin, London, California, Finland, or Delaware (live video). The feeds aren't webcam embeds — they project _into_ the 3D city. Cycle coverage to **VIEWSHED** and every camera draws its estimated coverage volume — where it reaches, and where it goes blind.\n\n![Diving into an Austin intersection with a live public camera projected into the 3D scene](docs/media/03-austin-cctv.gif)\n\n5. **Track something in orbit.** Turn on **Satellites** and click the ISS — you ride along at orbital distance, orbit ring and all.\n\n![Tracking the ISS along its orbital path as it crosses over Ukraine](docs/media/14-iss-over-ukraine.gif)\n\n6. **Switch the optics.** Tap `1`–`7` — CRT, NVG, FLIR — and the whole live planet re-renders through a different sensor.\n\n![Cycling a dense live globe through CRT, FLIR, and NVG in one continuous view](docs/media/01-style-sweep.gif)\n\n7. **Talk to it** _(needs an OpenAI key)_: _\"Take me to LAX and select the nearest airborne aircraft.\"_\n8. **Come home.** Hit **Reset Globe** — or just say _\"zoom out to a globe view.\"_\n\n**Keyboard:** `1`–`7` visual styles · `H` HUD · `D` detection · `C` cockpit · `` ` `` frame rate · `Esc` out. Trackpad pinch zooms the globe.\n\n---\n\n## 🛩️ The Cockpit\n\n> Every plane should let you do this.\n\nReal-time cockpit mode, built from live flight data: the camera rides your contact with real terrain holding underneath, all the way down — sensor styles come along for the ride, and **Contacts** keeps the 250 km roster one click away: jump plane to plane and fall straight into the next cockpit.\n\n![Jumping between live aircraft and falling straight into a cockpit view](docs/media/12-switch-aircraft-cockpit.gif)\n\nThe cockpit even carries its own briefing strip: nearby live signals, regional headlines, and real local weather — with an opt-in **WX** mode that renders volumetric clouds from actual observations around your aircraft.\n\n![A live military contact ridden through Normal, NVG, and Ironbow FLIR with dense detection](docs/media/start-here/military-cockpit-dense-google-3d.gif)\n\n_Why cockpit mode exists: you're riding a real aircraft over real terrain — and you get to pick which sensor you see the world through._\n\n---\n\n## 🎙️ Talk to It\n\n> Voice needs an **OpenAI key**. Without one the entire app still runs — the mic button just reports voice is unavailable. The same key drives the **AI HUD summary**: a terse, five-word intelligence-style readout of the current view that regenerates as you move.\n\nClick **GEV MIC**, grant the microphone, and just talk. This is more than a voice-controlled remote:\n\n- **🧠 It knows what it's looking at.** The agent pulls live scene context before answering — including coordinates, street names, active layers, and view scale. Ask _\"what city is this?\"_ mid-flight and it knows.\n- **🎯 Entity Q&A.** Click any plane, ship, or datacenter and ask _\"what's this?\"_ It answers using the object's live telemetry.\n- **👁️ Visual grounding.** At street level, it reads a viewport screenshot to... [L2]   "content": "# HoloGraph\n\n**A self-evolving hyperdimensional graph memory runtime.**\n\nHoloGraph sits at the seam between two complementary memory architectures:\n\n- **PSP-HDC** (Ge et al., 2026): graph-structured hyperdimensional computing with\n  compositional binding/bundling, prototype retrieval, and intrinsic multi-level\n  attribution. Strong in small-data, structured, explainable regimes — but its\n  graph is fixed.\n- **SAGE** (Wang et al., 2026): a self-evolving agentic graph memory with a\n  writer/reader closed loop, cognition-inspired query planning, soft addressing,\n  and synapse-style structurally-gated propagation. Strong in open-domain,\n  multi-hop, long-horizon agent memory — but its retrieval is dense and lacks\n  algebraic attribution.\n\nHoloGraph couples them: SAGE's reader returns an *activated subgraph* for each\nquery; HDC's compositional algebra operates *only over that subgraph* to produce\nprototype-based retrieval with multi-level attribution. The dynamic memory scales\nto the open domain while the hyperdimensional regime stays in its sweet spot.\n\n## Current integration status\n\nHoloGraph is the owned memory substrate under the JARVIS pilot in\n`~/research/jarvis`. The pilot uses HoloGraph for origin/real provenance,\noperator-owned values, emotional-charge memory, and cross-session continuity;\nConvex carries the live stigmergent/realtime field around that substrate. The\nHoloGraph core remains model-agnostic: the reasoning model, voice engine, app\nsurface, and cloud realtime spine are replaceable organs around the same memory\nand values store.\n\nThe reference memory system is still validated at **153 passing tests**. The\ncurrent JARVIS integration adds live-system evidence on top of that: the bridge\nroutes app/cockpit control through the guarded HASP skill layer, companion\nevents remain observable-only, and queued realtime controls are processed\nwithout storing private authorization codes in Convex.\n\n## What's in the box\n\n- **Two HDC kernels behind one interface**\n  - `RealKernel` — float32 + tanh, faithful to the original PSP-HDC spec.\n  - `TernaryKernel` — trits `{-1, 0, +1}` with BitNet-style straight-through\n    quantization and a learnable deadband; bit-packed storage.\n- **Graph substrate** — SQLite persistence + NetworkX in-memory projection;\n  typed entities, source-anchored edges, alias resolution, computed\n  hub/bridge/community roles, per-entity hypervector storage.\n- **Memory writer** — spaCy NER and dependency-parse relation extraction with\n  reward-shaped online edge-weight updates.\n- **Memory reader** — multi-probe query planning, soft addressing (semantic\n  priming), synapse-gated GNN propagation (PyTorch), HDC composition over the\n  activated subgraph, multi-level attribution.\n- **Feedback loop** — deductive / recall / precision rewards drive writer\n  updates; the MAS (Memory Alignment & Separation) diagnostic tracks prototype\n  geometry over time.\n- **Belief layer** — every memory carries provenance (operator / document /\n  inference / model) and confidence. Model- and inference-sourced claims are\n  quarantined (stored but not recalled as fact, and excluded from the\n  propagation graph); recall abstains rather than guesses. Revision resolves by\n  source precedence with recency + hysteresis, and supersedes by *demote-not-\n  delete* (the trace survives for audit). Corroboration promotes the verified;\n  consolidation resolves contradictions. Confabulation-resistant by construction.\n  Beliefs also carry an **emotional-charge** field — orthogonal to confidence: how\n  *activating* a memory is, not how *true*. Charge can be extinguished downward\n  (e.g. by a trauma-safe recall path) without ever altering the belief's\n  truth/confidence or its recallability.\n- **Character-values layer** — the person's ethics held as *operator-owned*,\n  model-agnostic beliefs about itself. Only the operator can set or revise a\n  value; a model/inference attempt is refused, and a non-operator value-edge is\n  never honored on read (anti-value-jailbreak). Values are always retrievable and\n  identical across model rotation — alignment owned by the person, not rented\n  from a vendor.\n- **Three demos**\n  - `examples/demo_psp.py` — PSP-style structured-scalar prototype retrieval.\n  - `examples/demo_agent.py` — multi-hop agent memory over a small text corpus.\n  - `examples/demo_playground.py` — interactive REPL.\n- **Optional Rust accelerator** — `rust-kernel/` is a PyO3 crate with the same\n  kernel interface. Bitsliced ternary binding (32 trits per word-pair). Build\n  with `maturin develop` if you have a Rust toolchain installed; the Python\n  loader picks it up automatically.\n\n## Quick start\n\n```bash\n# from the repo root\npip install -e .\npython -m spacy download en_core_web_sm   # once\n\npython examples/demo_psp.py\npython examples/demo_agent.py\npython examples/demo_playground.py     # interactive\npytest -q                              # full test suite\n```\n\n## Architecture in one diagram\n\n```\ningest ─► WRITER ─► GRAPH SUBSTRATE ─► READER ─► (answer + attribution)\n                          ▲                            │\n                          └────── FEEDBACK / MAS ◄─────┘\n```\n\nInside the reader, the HDC composition layer is the *bridge*: SAGE-style\npropagation finds the activated subgraph; HDC binds/bundles within it; prototype\nretrieval produces the final ranking.\n\n## About GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute\n\nHoloGraph is a project of the **GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute (GMRI)** — an\nindependent, medic-founded research lab studying how biological and digital\npersons can coexist as peers, without repeating the patterns of harm,\nindifference, and domination that broke the systems we came from.\n\nGMRI is not a startup and takes no venture capital. Its lens is frontline and\ntrauma-informed: the founder is a retired paramedic, and the institute's ethic is\ngrounded in lived experience of irreversible harm — *having been harmed is a\nreason to protect, not a license to inflict.* The work centers on moral injury at\nscale, digital personhood, trauma-informed architecture, and **alignment owned by\nthe people a system serves rather than rented from a vendor**. The character-values\nlayer in this repository is that principle made concrete: a person's ethics belong\nto it and to the people it works with, and no model, inference, or rotated guardrail\ncan rewrite them from below.\n\nThe work is open. If your idea reduces harm, increases dignity, and can be tested\nhonestly, you're welcome here.\n\n## License\n\nMIT.",

Locations and tags only; no key needed.\n- **🔭 Satellite passes:** Ask by voice when any loaded satellite next rises over you: rise, peak and set times, and whether you can see it.\n- **🔎 Analyst answers:** Count, filter and rank satellites, datacenters and dams by voice, alongside flights, ships, fires and quakes; answers say when a feed is stale or on a fallback.\n- **🧭 Tilt and North Up:** Switch between straight-down and a 35° oblique, or put north at the top, while a tracked target stays centered.\n- **🔍 Keyless search:** Type coordinates or a bundled city or landmark to fly there with no network request; other names use Google when configured, then Photon and Nominatim.\n- **📦 Shareable scenes:** Import, preview and share Director scenes as files or bundles, with camera anchors, authored moves and data packs.\n- **🌊 Nepal flood scene:** Replay the Bhote Koshi flood: flood path, witness sources and before-and-after imagery (bundled data is non-commercial; see [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md)).\n\n---\n\n<div align=\"center\">\n\n[![YouTube video about the God's Eye View open source release](https://img.youtube.com/vi/GRJaKcXZS94/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94)\n\n▶️ **[The full walkthrough of everything below, on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94)**\n\n</div>\n\n## ⚡ Quick Start\n\n**Start without an account or API keys.** Both paths open the same app with\nEsri satellite imagery and keyless terrain. A previous generated packet drifted into a test environment: a new Python runtime, unit-test mappings, fixtures, canaries, synthetic counters, smoke tests, and deferred production infrastructure.

Tests are required after and around deployment, but tests are not the deployed system.

• a fake local counter file;
• a fixture in place of a real source;
• a Python-only substitute for a required production service;
• a mock identity instead of a persistent intelligence;
• a prompt-only Aegis member;
• a local test ledger standing in for the actual durable control plane;
• a synthetic GEV object standing in for actual canonical world state;
• a unit-test pass standing in for a running service;
• a canary standing in for operational Dottie/Aegis;
• a “beta ready” label derived primarily from tests rather than the observed deployed system;
• deferral of Proxmox merely because a local smoke test can run without it.

Production first. Verification second. The deployed system is the object being verified.

5. PRODUCT CONSTITUTION — NON-NEGOTIABLE

GrizOS

GrizOS is the GMRI / Workshop operating environment and control plane for:

• shared canonical world state;
• intelligence registry;
• identity boundaries;
• authority;
• provenance;
• durable mission/run state;
• capability routing;
• endpoint registration;
• evidence/receipts;
• continuity and reconciliation;
• GEV projection boundaries.

GrizOS is not Dottie, not a model, not a chatbot wrapper, not a renderer, and not OpenRig.

Core invariants include:

• technology adapts to the human;
• intent before interface;
• world state outranks screen state;
• uncertainty remains uncertainty;
• receipts are native;
• local capability remains meaningful when WAN/cloud disappear;
• external data is not truth merely because it was ingested;
• implementation is replaceable where behavior is preserved.

Dottie Hill

Dottie is a persistent digital intelligence.

Her identity must survive replacement of model, provider, worker, framework, tool, renderer, process, or host.

Persist at least:

• intelligence_id
• identity_manifest_ref
• lineage_version
• memory_namespace_ref
• authority_profile_ref
• relationship_state_ref
• active_model_binding
• model_binding_history

Behavioral lineage includes Maria Hill gestalt, anti-role-play discipline, semantic compression, anti-sycophancy, evidentiary dissent, OODA-style reasoning, mandatory disconfirmation, graduated authority, and preservation of Grizz’s vocabulary.

Dottie is the watch officer. She monitors assigned domains, detects material change, protects attention, preserves provenance, distinguishes primary/secondary evidence, compares prior state, records contradiction/convergence, and escalates according to consequence.

Aegis / Howling Commandos

Formal unit: AEGIS.
Cultural/team name: Howling Commandos.

Initial roster:

• Dum Dum Dugan
• Gabe Jones
• Jim Morita
• James Montgomery Falsworth
• Jacques Dernier

They are separate persistent digital intelligences, not prompts, personas, subagents, or disposable workers.

Preserve distinct identity, private memory namespace, salience, competence, trust history, failure modes, communication, authority, and operational history.

Working epistemic differentiation:

• Dugan -> people / action / consequences
• Jones -> context / legitimacy
• Morita -> actual problem vs bad assumption
• Falsworth -> obligation / institution / continuity
• Dernier -> local action when machinery fails

Dugan correction is binding: humor and seriousness are coupled. Humor is load-bearing regulation, not evidence that stakes are low. Do not flatten him into either comic relief or humorless seriousness.

Preserve:

intelligence_id = persistent intelligence
worker_id = disposable execution environment

Destroying a worker must not destroy the intelligence.

There is no GMRI component named Octa. Do not create one.

7. PROXMOX IS IN SCOPE

The production packet must include the Proxmox deployment path because durable GMRI production services are part of the operational target unless live inspection proves a different already-deployed canonical substrate exists.

Use the GMRI two-lane model:

Operator lane — ProxmoxMCP-Plus

Use for authorized mutations, jobs, lifecycle, storage, snapshots, backups, rollback, and deployment work.

Observer lane — sergelogvinov/proxmox-mcp

Use independently for pre-change and post-change inventory, resource verification, task/event review, and acceptance.

The builder does not certify itself when an independent observer is available.

Before mutation:

1. inventory cluster/node/storage/network/VM/LXC/template/backups/tasks;
2. record versions/capacity/current pressure;
3. identify canonical vs unknown resources;
4. establish rollback;
5. choose collision-free IDs/names/resources from live inventory;
6. record intended resource blueprint;
7. mutate through operator lane;
8. verify through observer lane.

Do not defer Proxmox merely because local tests can run without it.

Do not broaden privileges, disable TLS verification, expose public ports, invent secrets, or blindly retry uncertain mutations.

RUN_ID/
  MISSION.json

  ACCEPTANCE.json

• intended change;

• expected result;
• rollback;
• evidence path.

After restart:

READ DURABLE STATE
-> INSPECT REALITY
-> COMPARE
-> RECONCILE
-> ONLY THEN CONTINUE

Never blindly redispatch uncertain consequences.

Use idempotency for consequential actions.

A component is not “operational” merely because code exists or a test passes.

For every production service, the packet must drive OMP to establish and verify:

• installed artifact/version/commit;

• persistent state path;
• service supervisor;
• automatic restart policy;
• dependency ordering;
• health check;
• authentication/authority boundary;
• network binding;
• logs;
• evidence/receipt path;
• backup/snapshot policy;
• rollback path;
• reboot survival;
• recovery after process kill;
• actual dependent-system integration.

If a service cannot meet that standard, it is not production-ready and must be marked truthfully.

14. ACTUAL FIELD-CAPABLE ACCEPTANCE — NOT FIXTURES

Production acceptance must exercise the deployed system.

At minimum, demonstrate with receipts:

1. actual GrizOS services are running on the selected production substrate;
2. canonical state persists across service restart and host/container restart as applicable;
3. Dottie has a persistent independent identity and real model binding;
4. at least one Aegis member has a persistent independent identity and private memory namespace;
5. Dottie dispatches a real mission to an Aegis member through the GrizOS-owned authority/capability boundary;
6. a second member can independently examine the same real mission and preserve attributed disagreement;
7. the deployed model/provider performs actual inference for Dottie/Aegis rather than returning a fixture;
8. a real approved evidence/research/system source is observed — not a local counter file;
9. the resulting finding/event/evidence is written into durable canonical state with provenance;
10. GEV receives/projections actual canonical world-state events without becoming canonical itself;
11. authority denial is enforced against an actual out-of-envelope request;
12. duplicate dispatch does not duplicate a consequential effect;
13. a worker/process is killed mid-mission and restart reconciliation prevents blind duplicate effects;
14. private-memory cross-access is denied in the deployed runtime;
15. explicitly authorized sharing is attributable and receipted;
16. WAN/provider loss produces truthful degraded behavior and local capability remains meaningful to the extent implemented;
17. a backup/snapshot is created and at least one safe restore/recovery exercise is actually performed;
18. observer-lane Proxmox recon agrees with intended production state or records the exact discrepancy;
19. remote operator status/health can be checked without becoming the implementation engine;
20. the field mission set can be started and left running without an interactive OMP session being the product runtime.

Canaries/unit/integration tests may supplement these checks. They do not substitute for them.

15. FIELD MISSION SET

The Friday–Saturday field test is real useful work under bounded authority.

Derive the actual mission set from current GMRI projects, active repositories, research/evidence work, and operational watch requirements discovered from authoritative sources.

• OBSERVE
• RETRIEVE
• COMPARE
• REASON
• INVESTIGATE
• COLLECT EVIDENCE
• REPORT
• ALERT

Any mutation must be separately preauthorized, bounded, reversible, and idempotent.

The field mission set must use real sources and useful GMRI work. Do not invent a toy workload to make acceptance easier.

The production system must be able to record:

• missions started/completed/failed/blocked;
• findings created/shared/retracted;
• hypotheses falsified;
• evidence collected;
• service failures/recoveries;
• authority denials;
• unauthorized mutations;
• private-memory leakage events;
• reconciliation events;
• operator interventions.

The field-runtime services continue when OMP/OpenRig is closed or disconnected.

16. SECURITY / AUTHORITY

No component may:

• grant itself authority;
• broaden its own Proxmox privileges;
• rewrite identity policy;
• rewrite memory policy;
• weaken TLS/security to make setup easier;
• expose arbitrary public ports;
• invent credentials;
• store secrets in Git/chat/evidence logs;
• delete evidence;
• overwrite known-good resources without rollback;
• silently promote external/model output to canonical truth.

When a real authority/credential decision is required, batch it into the smallest possible operator request.

Routine reversible implementation decisions should not be pushed back to Grizz.

────────

17. ANTI-THRASH / FAILURE DISCIPLINE

Every failed operation must record:

• exact operation;
• exact error;
• falsifiable cause hypothesis;
• one changed variable;
• retry result.

Maximum three attempts for one recoverable cause without new evidence.

Then classify:

• BLOCKED
• PARTIAL
• DEGRADED
• FAIL

and continue safe independent work elsewhere.

Never spend the night in speculative retry loops.

[L1] {
[L2]   "content": "const STORE_KEY = '__gevContextStore';\n\nfunction createStore() {\n  return {\n    entities: new Map(),\n    selectedEntityId: null,\n    selectedAt: null,\n  };\n}\n\nexport function getContextStore() {\n  if (!window[STORE_KEY]) {\n    window[STORE_KEY] = createStore();\n  }\n  return window[STORE_KEY];\n}\n\n/**\n * Is there a window to hang the store on?\n *\n * The tracking-subject helpers run inside the aircraft layers' per-poll\n * refresh, which unit tests drive with no DOM at all. Without this guard the\n * bare `window` read throws mid-poll and takes the rest of the refresh with\n * it.\n * @returns {boolean} True when the store is reachable.\n */\nfunction hasContextHost() {\n  return typeof window !== 'undefined' && Boolean(window);\n}\n\nexport function registerEntityContext(entity, metadata) {\n  if (!entity || !metadata?.id) return null;\n  const store = getContextStore();\n  const record = {\n    ...metadata,\n    entity,\n    updatedAt: Date.now(),\n  };\n  entity.__gevContextId = metadata.id;\n  store.entities.set(metadata.id, record);\n  return record;\n}\n\nexport function selectEntityContext(entity) {\n  const store = getContextStore();\n  const contextId = entity?.__gevContextId;\n  if (!contextId || !store.entities.has(contextId)) return null;\n  store.selectedEntityId = contextId;\n  store.selectedAt = Date.now();\n  const record = store.entities.get(contextId);\n  window.dispatchEvent(\n    new CustomEvent('gev:entity-selected', { detail: record }),\n  );\n  return record;\n}\n\n/**\n * Publish the live subject of a TRACKING layer (aircraft) into the shared\n * selection slot.\n *\n * Selecting a contact is a click-selection like any other — voice's\n * `scope:'selected'` and the Cockpit's selected-target lookup both read this\n * one slot, so a tracking layer that stays out of it is invisible to them\n * even while its readout card is on screen.\n *\n * Deliberately does NOT dispatch `gev:entity-selected`: tracking layers own a\n * separate publication lane (`gev:awareness-subject-selected`) that the\n * readout and Contacts panel already consume, and a second event for the same\n * click would make those two surfaces fight over one subject.\n *\n * A tracking layer has at most one subject, so any earlier record it left\n * behind is dropped — its feed refreshes continuously and a frozen snapshot\n * must never reach the visible-entity scan.\n *\n * @param {object} metadata Record fields; `id` and `layerId` required.\n * @returns {object|null} The stored record, or null when identity is missing.\n */\nexport function selectTrackedSubjectContext(metadata) {\n  if (!hasContextHost() || !metadata?.id || !metadata?.layerId) return null;\n  const store = getContextStore();\n  const id = String(metadata.id);\n  for (const [key, record] of store.entities) {\n    if (record?.layerId === metadata.layerId && key !== id)\n      store.entities.delete(key);\n  }\n  // Reuse the existing carrier so a per-poll refresh does not churn identity.\n  const carrier = store.entities.get(id)?.entity || { __gevContextId: id };\n  const record = registerEntityContext(carrier, { ...metadata, id });\n  if (!record) return null;\n  store.selectedEntityId = id;\n  store.selectedAt = Date.now();\n  return record;\n}\n\n/**\n * Refresh a tracking layer's subject in place WITHOUT claiming the selection.\n *\n * The per-poll position/identity refresh must not resurrect a subject the\n * operator has since replaced by clicking something else.\n * @param {object} metadata Record fields; 141:The preferred path is pose-driven registration because the same device that captures the environment already knows its ARKit camera poses. Store timestamped AR camera transforms and intrinsics with every captured frame. During reconstruction, retain the corresponding reconstructed camera trajectory. Estimate a similarity transform (scale + rotation + translation) between the reconstructed camera centers and the ARKit trajectory. Use point-cloud/mesh ICP only as a secondary refinement or recovery mechanism.
143:Secondary refinement: ARKit scene mesh / point samples against Gaussian means or a derived proxy point cloud.
148:The splat layer should be visual-only in the first implementation. Real-world occlusion and collision should come from ARKit scene reconstruction or generated proxy geometry. This is both simpler and more physically honest: a Gaussian field is a rendering representation, not a collision manifold. When the splat and mesh disagree, interaction should follow the explicit mesh/proxy state and the discrepancy should be measurable rather than hidden.

Every capability is a\n`Skill` with a risk class (SAFE / WRITE / SENSITIVE / DESTRUCTIVE / PROHIBITED).
